Compression for quantum population coding

Abstract

We study the compression of arbitrary parametric families of nn identically prepared finite-dimensional quantum states, in a setting that can be regarded as a quantum analogue of population coding. For a family with ff free parameters, we propose an asymptotically faithful protocol that requires a memory of overall size (f/2)​log⁡n(f/2)\log n. Our construction uses a quantum version of local asymptotic normality and, as an intermediate step, solves the problem of the optimal compression of nn identically prepared displaced thermal states. Our protocol achieves the ultimate bound predicted by quantum Shannon theory. In addition, we explore the minimum requirement for quantum memory: On the one hand, the amount of quantum memory used by our protocol can be made arbitrarily small compared to the overall memory cost; on the other hand, any protocol using only classical memory cannot be faithful.

Index Terms: 
population coding, compression, quantum system, local asymptotic normality, identically prepared state

I Introduction

Many problems in quantum information theory involve a source that prepares multiple copies of the same quantum state. This is the case, for example, of quantum tomography [1], quantum cloning [2, 3], and quantum state discrimination [4]. The state prepared by the source is generally unknown to the agent who has to carry out the task. Instead, the agent knows that the state belongs to some parametric family of density matrices {ρθ}θ∈Θ\{\rho_{\theta}\}_{\theta\in\Theta}, with the parameter θ\theta varying in the set Θ\Theta. Also, it is promised that all the particles emitted by the source are independently prepared in the same quantum state ρθ\rho_{\theta}: when the source is used nn times, it generates nn quantum particles in the tensor product state ρθ⊗n\rho_{\theta}^{\otimes n}.

How much information is contained in the nn-particle state ρθ⊗n\rho_{\theta}^{\otimes n}? One way to address this question is to quantify the minimum amount of memory needed to store the state. Solving this problem requires an optimization over all possible compression protocols. When the number of copies is large, it is tempting to use a classical protocol, wherein the parameter θ\theta is estimated and the estimate is stored in a classical memory. However, this type of storage is generally not faithful, as shown in [5] for several examples of pure state families. In order to achieve a faithful storage, a non-zero amount of quantum memory is generally required. It is important to stress that the problem of storing the nn-copy states {ρθ⊗n,θ∈Θ}\{\rho_{\theta}^{\otimes n}\,,\,\theta\in\Theta\} in a quantum memory is different from the standard problem of quantum data compression [6, 7, 8]. In our scenario, the mixed state ρθ\rho_{\theta} is not regarded as the average state of an information source, but, instead, as a physical encoding of the parameter θ\theta. The goal of compression is to preserve the encoding of the parameter θ\theta, by storing the state ρθ⊗n\rho_{\theta}^{\otimes n} into a memory and retrieving it with high fidelity for all possible values of θ\theta. To stress the difference with standard quantum compression, we refer to our scenario as compression for quantum population coding. The expression “quantum population coding” refers to the encoding of the parameter θ\theta into the many-particle state ρθ⊗n\rho_{\theta}^{\otimes n}. We choose this expression in analogy with (classical) population coding, whereby a parameter is encoded into the population of nn individuals [9]. The typical example of population coding arises in computational neuroscience, where the population consists of neurons and the parameter represents an external stimulus.

The compression for quantum population coding has been studied by Plesch and Bužek [10] in the case where ρθ\rho_{\theta} is a pure qubit state and no error is tolerated (see also [11] for a prototype experimental implementation). A first extension to mixed states, higher dimensions, and non-zero error was proposed by some of us in [12]. The protocol therein was proven to be optimal under the assumption that the decoding operation must satisfy a suitable conservation law. Later, a new protocol that reaches the ultimate information-theoretic bound was found for qubit states [13]. The classical version of the problem was addressed in [14]. However, finding the optimal protocol for arbitrary parametric families of quantum states has remained as an open problem so far.

In this paper, we provide the general theory for the compression of nn-tensor product state in a quantum parametric state family. We consider two categories of state families: families of finite-dimensional states and displaced thermal families of infinite-dimensional states. These two categories of state families turn out to be connected by the quantum version of local asymptotic normality (Q-LAN)[15, 16, 17, 18], which reduces nn-tensor product of a finite-dimensional state locally to a displaced thermal state. As the first step, we discuss this kind of compression for the thermal states family, which can be regarded as the quantum extension of the Gaussian distribution. In the next step, employing Q-LAN, we reduce the problem of compressing generic finite-dimensional states to the case of displaced thermal states. Unlike previous works, our protocol does not require any assumption on the symmetry of the state family. In addition, an intriguing feature of this protocol is that the ratio between the size of quantum memory and the size of classical memory can be made arbitrarily close to but not equal to zero. Such a feature is not an incidence but an essence: for identically prepared displaced thermal states and qudit states, we show that any compression protocol using only classical memory must have non-vanishing error.

The rest of the paper is structured as follows. In Section III we study the compression of displaced thermal states. In Section IV we propose a protocol for the compression of identically prepared finite-dimensional states. Optimality of the protocols is proven later in Section VI. In Section V we show that it is necessary to use quantum memory to achieve faithful compression. Finally, we conclude the paper by some discussions in Section VII.

II Main result.

The main result of our work is the optimal compression of identically prepared quantum states. We consider two major categories of states: finite dimensional (i.e. qudit) states and displaced thermal states. The key question addressed here is how much memory is needed at least to encode the states, in a way that they can be recovered with an error vanishing in the number of input copies. The memory cost essentially depends on the (sub)family from which the states are drawn. For instance, the memory cost for diagonal qudit states (i.e. classical probability distributions) should be less than the cost for general qudit states. As a consequence, we need to define the state subfamilies being considered before stating the main result.

We begin by introducing the parameterization for d(<∞)d(<\infty)-dimensional non-degenerate quantum systems, whose states can be generated by rotating a fixed state ρ0​(μ)\rho_{0}(\mu) with spectrum μ\mu, i.e.

ρθ\displaystyle\rho_{\theta} =Uξ​ρ0​(μ)​Uξ†\displaystyle=U_{\xi}\rho_{0}(\mu)U^{\dagger}_{\xi} (1)

where

Uξ\displaystyle U_{\xi} =exp⁡[i⁡(∑1≤j<k≤dξj,kR​Tj,k+ξj,kI​Tk,jμj−μk)]\displaystyle=\exp\left[i\left(\sum_{1\leq j<k\leq d}\frac{\xi^{R}_{j,k}T_{j,k}+\xi^{I}_{j,k}T_{k,j}}{\sqrt{\mu_{j}-\mu_{k}}}\right)\right] (2)
Tj,k\displaystyle T_{j,k} =i​Ej,k−i​Ek,jTk,j=Ej,k+Ek,j\displaystyle=iE_{j,k}-iE_{k,j}\qquad T_{k,j}=E_{j,k}+E_{k,j} (3)

Therefore, any non-degenerate qudit state can be parameterized as ρθ\rho_{\theta}, where θ=(μ,ξ)∈ℝd2−1\theta=(\mu,\xi)\in\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}-1} is a vector of parameters with μ=(μ1,μ2,…,μd−1)\mu=(\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\dots,\mu_{d-1}) being its spectrum, ordered as μ1>⋯>μd−1>0\mu_{1}>\cdots>\mu_{d-1}>0, and ξ=(…,ξj,kR,ξj,kI,…)​(1≤j<k≤d)\xi=(\dots,\xi^{R}_{j,k},\xi^{I}_{j,k},\dots)(1\leq j<k\leq d) being the rotation parameters. A qudit state (sub)family will be denoted as {ρθ⊗n}θ∈Θ\{\rho_{\theta}^{\otimes n}\}_{\theta\in\mathsf{\Theta}} with Θ=Θ1×Θ2×⋯×Θd2−1\mathsf{\Theta}=\mathsf{\Theta}_{1}\times\mathsf{\Theta}_{2}\times\cdots\times\mathsf{\Theta}_{d^{2}-1} where Θi\mathsf{\Theta}_{i} is the range of the ii-th component of θ\theta. For simplicity of discussion, we assume Θi=[ai,ai′]\mathsf{\Theta}_{i}=[a_{i},a^{\prime}_{i}] for ai,ai′∈ℝa_{i},a^{\prime}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}. We call a component of μ\mu a free classical parameter if its range is [μi,μi′][\mu_{i},\mu^{\prime}_{i}] for μi′>μi\mu^{\prime}_{i}>\mu_{i} and a component of ξ\xi a free quantum parameter if its range is [ξi,ξi′][\xi_{i},\xi^{\prime}_{i}] for ξi′>ξi\xi^{\prime}_{i}>\xi_{i}. Otherwise the range set of the parameter contains only one value and the parameter is fixed. We denote by fcf_{c} (fqf_{q}) the number of free classical (quantum) parameters of the (sub)family.

Next we introduce displaced thermal states, which are a type of states frequently encountered in quantum optics. Displaced thermal states can be regarded as coherent states subject to Gaussian additive noise. A coherent state, describing the state of a laser under ideal conditions, is parametrized as

|α⟩=e−|α|22​∑k=0∞αkk!​|k⟩α=|α|​ei​TT∈[0,2​π),\displaystyle|\alpha\rangle=e^{-\frac{|\alpha|^{2}}{2}}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{\alpha^{k}}{\sqrt{k!}}|k\rangle\qquad\alpha=|\alpha|e^{iT}\quad T\in[0,2\pi)\,,

where {|k⟩}\{|k\rangle\} is the photon number basis. Gaussian additive noise is described by the quantum channel (completely positive trace preserving map)

𝒩β​(ρ)=∫d2μ⁡(1−βπ​β)​e−(1−β)​|μ|2β​Dμ​ρ​Dμ†\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{\beta}(\rho)=\int\mathop{\rm d}\nolimits^{2}\mu\,\left(\frac{1-\beta}{\pi\beta}\right)e^{-\frac{(1-\beta)|\mu|^{2}}{\beta}}\,D_{\mu}\,\rho D_{\mu}^{\dagger} (4)

where Dμ=exp⁡(μ​a^†−μ¯​a^)D_{\mu}=\exp(\mu\hat{a}^{\dagger}-\bar{\mu}\hat{a}) is the displacement operator and β∈[0,1)\beta\in[0,1) is a suitable parameter. When applied to an input coherent state, the Gaussian additive noise outputs the displaced thermal state

ρα,β=Dα​ρβ(thm)​Dα†α=|α|​ei​TT∈[0,2​π),\displaystyle\rho_{\alpha,\beta}=D_{\alpha}\,\rho^{({\rm thm})}_{\beta}D^{\dagger}_{\alpha}\qquad\alpha=|\alpha|e^{iT}\quad T\in[0,2\pi), (5)

with

ρβ(thm)\displaystyle\rho^{({\rm thm})}_{\beta} =𝒩β​(|0⟩​⟨0|)=(1−β)​∑i=0∞βi​|i⟩​⟨i|.\displaystyle=\mathcal{N}_{\beta}(|0\rangle\langle 0|)=(1-\beta)\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\beta^{i}|i\rangle\langle i|\,. (6)

We consider a (sub)family of nn identically prepared displaced thermal states, denoted by {ρα,β⊗n}(β,α)∈Θ\{\rho_{\alpha,\beta}^{\otimes n}\}_{(\beta,\alpha)\in\mathsf{\Theta}} with Θ=Θβ×Θα\mathsf{\Theta}=\mathsf{\Theta}_{\beta}\times\mathsf{\Theta}_{\alpha} being the parameter space. Similar as the qudit state case, there are three real parameters for the displaced thermal state family: the thermal parameter β\beta, the strength of the displacement |α||\alpha|, and the phase T=arg⁡αT=\arg\alpha. β\beta is a classical parameter, specifying the probability distribution of the eigenvalues, while |α||\alpha| and TT are quantum parameters, determining the eigenstates of the density matrix. Each of the three parameters is free if its range is [a,b][a,b] for a<ba<b, otherwise we assume that the range set contains only a single value and the parameter is fixed. Again, we denote by fcf_{c} (fqf_{q}) the number of free classical (quantum) parameters of the (sub)family.

A compression protocol consists of two components: the encoder, which compresses the input state into a memory, and the decoder, which recovers the state from the memory. A protocol is thus represented by a couple of quantum channels (completely positive trace-preserving linear maps) (ℰ,𝒟)(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{D}) characterizing the encoder and the decoder, respectively. We focus on faithful compression protocols, whose error vanishes in the large nn limit. As a measure of error, we choose the supremum of the trace distance between the original state and the recovered state 𝒟∘ℰ⁡(ρθ⊗n)\mathcal{D}\circ\mathcal{E}(\rho_{\theta}^{\otimes n})

ϵ:=supθ∈Θ12​‖ρθ⊗n−𝒟∘ℰ⁡(ρθ⊗n)‖1.\displaystyle\epsilon:=\sup_{\theta\in\mathsf{\Theta}}\frac{1}{2}\|\rho_{\theta}^{\otimes n}-\mathcal{D}\circ\mathcal{E}(\rho_{\theta}^{\otimes n})\|_{1}\,. (7)

The main result of our work is the following:

Theorem 1.

Let {ρθ⊗n}θ=(μ,ξ)∈Θ\{\rho_{\theta}^{\otimes n}\}_{\theta=(\mu,\xi)\in\mathsf{\Theta}} be the state (sub)family of nn identical displaced thermal states or non-degenerate qudit states with fcf_{c} free classical parameters and fqf_{q} free quantum parameters. For any δ∈(0,2/9)\delta\in(0,2/9), the state family can be compressed into [(1/2+δ)​fc+(1/2)​fq]​log⁡n[(1/2+\delta)f_{c}+(1/2)f_{q}]\log n classical bits and (fq​δ)​log⁡n(f_{q}\delta)\log n qubits with an error ϵ=O(n−δ/2)+O(n−κ⁡(δ))\epsilon=O\left(n^{-\delta/2}\right)+O\left(n^{-\kappa(\delta)}\right), where κ⁡(δ)\kappa(\delta) is the error of Q-LAN [18] given by Eq. (26). The compression is optimal, in the sense that any compression protocol requiring a memory of size [(fc+fq)/2−δ′]​log⁡n[(f_{c}+f_{q})/2-\delta^{\prime}]\log n with δ′>0\delta^{\prime}>0 cannot be faithful.

Theorem 1 states that to encode each free parameter a memory of size (1/2+δ)​log⁡n(1/2+\delta)\log n is required. When the parameter is classical, the required memory is fully classical; when the parameter is quantum, a quantum memory of δ​log⁡n\delta\log n qubits is required. Note that Theorem 1 solves the compression of several important (sub)families:

  • •

    The full model family of qudits (fc=d−1f_{c}=d-1 and fq=d⁡(d−1)f_{q}=d(d-1)).

  • •

    The classical qudit subfamily (fc=d−1f_{c}=d-1 and fq=0f_{q}=0) of dd-dimensional classical probability distributions can be compressed into (d/2)​log⁡n(d/2)\log n classical bits, retrieving the result of [14].

  • •

    The phase-covariant qudit subfamily (fc=d−1f_{c}=d-1 and fq=d⁡(d−1)/2f_{q}=d(d-1)/2), where ξj,kI=0\xi^{I}_{j,k}=0 for any jj, kk.

III Compression of displaced thermal states.

In this section, we consider the compression of identically prepared displaced thermal states ρα,β⊗n\rho^{\otimes n}_{\alpha,\beta} for 8 different subfamilies, corresponding to cases when β\beta, |α||\alpha| and TT are either free or fixed. The memory costs are summarized in Table I, which matches the statement of Theorem 1. For instance, in Case 5 we have fq=1f_{q}=1 (TT is a quantum parameter) and fc=1f_{c}=1 (β\beta is a classical parameter), and therefore the memory costs are δ​log⁡n\delta\log n qubits and (1+δ)​log⁡n(1+\delta)\log n bits. On the other hand, the errors for all cases satisfy the unified bound

ϵ=O(n−δ/2).\displaystyle\epsilon=O\left(n^{-\delta/2}\right).

We now show details of the compression protocol for each case. Since Case 0 (all parameters are fixed) is essentially trivial, we start from Case 1, where only β\beta is a free parameter.

III-A Case 1: free β\beta; fixed α\alpha.

An important property for nn identically displaced thermal states is that they are equivalent, up to an unitary transformation, to a product of thermal states where the displacement appears only on one mode, namely

UBS​ρα,β⊗n​UBS†=ρn​α,β⊗(ρβ(thm))⊗(n−1),\displaystyle U_{\rm BS}\,\rho_{\alpha,\beta}^{\otimes n}\,U^{\dagger}_{\rm BS}=\rho_{\sqrt{n}\alpha,\beta}\otimes\left(\rho^{({\rm thm})}_{\beta}\right)^{\otimes(n-1)}\,, (8)

where UBSU_{\rm BS} is a unitary operator, which can be physically implemented through a suitable arrangement of beam splitters [19, 20]. Using this property, we can construct a protocol that separately compresses the displaced thermal state ρn​α,β\rho_{\sqrt{n}\alpha,\beta} and the n−1n-1 thermal modes. For the compression of the thermal modes, we have the following lemma.

Lemma 1 (Compression of identically prepared thermal states).

For any x>0x>0, there exists a protocol (ℰn,x(thm),𝒟n,x(thm))\left(\mathcal{E}^{({\rm thm})}_{n,x},\mathcal{D}^{({\rm thm})}_{n,x}\right) compressing nn copies of a thermal state ρβ(thm)\rho^{({\rm thm})}_{\beta} into (1/2+x)​log⁡n(1/2+x)\log n classical bits with error

ϵthm=O⁡(n−x).\displaystyle\epsilon_{\rm thm}=O\left(n^{-x}\right). (9)

The proof of the above lemma can be found in Appendix. We emphasize that no quantum memory is required to encode thermal states. For any δ>0\delta>0, we can then construct the compression protocol as follows:

  • •

    Encoder.

    1. 1.

      First perform on each input copy the displacement operation 𝒟−α\mathcal{D}_{-\alpha}, defined by

      𝒟μ​(⋅):=Dμ⋅Dμ†\mathcal{D}_{\mu}(\cdot):={D}_{\mu}\cdot{D}_{\mu}^{\dagger}

      where Dμ=exp⁡(μ​a^†−μ¯​a^)D_{\mu}=\exp(\mu\hat{a}^{\dagger}-\bar{\mu}\hat{a}) is the displacement operator. The displacement operation transforms each input copy ρα,β\rho_{\alpha,\beta} into the thermal state ρβ(thm)\rho^{({\rm thm})}_{\beta}.

    2. 2.

      Then apply the thermal state encoder ℰn,δ(thm)\mathcal{E}^{({\rm thm})}_{n,\delta} on the nn-mode state and the outcome is encoded in a classical memory.

  • •

    Decoder.

    1. 1.

      First use the thermal state decoder 𝒟n,δ(thm)\mathcal{D}^{({\rm thm})}_{n,\delta} to recover the nn copies of the thermal state ρβ(thm)\rho^{({\rm thm})}_{\beta} from the classical memory.

    2. 2.

      Perform the displacement operation 𝒟α\mathcal{D}_{\alpha} on each mode.

Note that the input state can be regarded as the state of nn optical modes with each mode in a displaced thermal state, and thus the compression protocol can be regarded as a sequence of operations on the nn-mode system. We shall use the term “mode” throughout this section.

The above protocol requires only (1/2+δ)​log⁡n(1/2+\delta)\log n bits for any δ>0\delta>0 by Lemma 1. The error is also the same as in Lemma 1, for the displacement operations are unitary.

III-B Case 2: unknown α\alpha, fixed β\beta.

Next we study the more involved case when the displacement α\alpha is unknown. Let us first look at the idea how to compress before going into details of the compression protocol. To save as much quantum memory as possible, we may consider to estimate α\alpha and store the outcome in a classical memory. However, any estimate of α\alpha comes at the price of disturbing the input state, and, as shown later in Section V, the distortion caused by measurements on all input copies is so large that the state cannot be recovered faithfully. Instead of full measurements, here we adopt a strategy of measuring only a small portion of the input copies so that we still get an estimate of α\alpha, while the distortion can still be recovered. We then perform coherent quantum protocols based on the information gained by the estimation. Such an idea of gently testing the input state and then performing coherent compression is key to this work, which allows us to convert the memory cost from quantum to classical as much as possible.

For any δ>0\delta>0, the protocol runs as follows:

  • •

    Preprocessing. A preprocessing procedure is needed in order to store the estimate of α\alpha: Divide the range of α\alpha into nn zones, each labeled by a point α^i\hat{\alpha}_{i} in it, so that |α′−α′′|=O(n−1/2)|\alpha^{\prime}-\alpha^{\prime\prime}|=O(n^{-1/2}) (note that α\alpha is complex) for any α′,α′′\alpha^{\prime},\alpha^{\prime\prime} in the same zone.

  • •

    Encoder.

    1. 1.

      First perform the unitary channel 𝒰BS​(⋅)=UBS⋅UBS†\mathcal{U}_{\rm BS}(\cdot)=U_{\rm BS}\,\cdot\,U_{\rm BS}^{\dagger} on the input state, where UBSU_{\rm BS} is the unitary defined by Eq. (8). The output state has the form ρn​α,β⊗(ρβ(thm))⊗(n−1)\rho_{\sqrt{n}\alpha,\beta}\otimes\left(\rho^{({\rm thm})}_{\beta}\right)^{\otimes(n-1)}.

    2. 2.

      Send the first and the last mode through a beam splitter with transitivity n−δn^{-\delta}. The nn-mode state is now ρn−n1−δ​α,β⊗(ρβ(thm))⊗(n−2)⊗ρn1−δ​α,β\rho_{\sqrt{n-n^{1-\delta}}\alpha,\beta}\otimes\left(\rho^{({\rm thm})}_{\beta}\right)^{\otimes(n-2)}\otimes\rho_{\sqrt{n^{1-\delta}}\alpha,\beta}.

    3. 3.

      Estimate α\alpha by the heterodyne measurement {d2α′​|α′⟩​⟨α′|}\{\mathop{\rm d}\nolimits^{2}\alpha^{\prime}|\alpha^{\prime}\rangle\langle\alpha^{\prime}|\} on the last mode, which yields an estimate α^=α′/n1−δ\hat{\alpha}=\alpha^{\prime}/\sqrt{n^{1-\delta}} with the probability distribution

      Q⁡(α^|α)=(1−β)​exp⁡[−(1−β)​n1−δ​|α^−α|2].\displaystyle Q(\hat{\alpha}|\alpha)=(1-\beta)\exp[-(1-\beta)n^{1-\delta}|\hat{\alpha}-\alpha|^{2}]. (10)

      Encode the label of the zone α^∗\hat{\alpha}^{\ast} containing α^\hat{\alpha} in a classical memory.

    4. 4.

      Displace the first mode with 𝒟−n−n1−δ​α^∗\mathcal{D}_{-\sqrt{n-n^{1-\delta}}\hat{\alpha}^{\ast}}.

    5. 5.

      The state of the first mode then goes through a truncation in the photon number basis, described by the channel 𝒫n2​δ\mathcal{P}_{n^{2\delta}} defined as

      𝒫n2​δ​(ρ)=Pn2​δ​ρ​Pn2​δ+(1−Tr[Pn2​δ​ρ])​|0⟩​⟨0|\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{n^{2\delta}}(\rho)={P}_{n^{2\delta}}\rho{P}_{n^{2\delta}}+(1-\mathop{\rm Tr}\nolimits[{P}_{n^{2\delta}}\rho])|0\rangle\langle 0| (11)

      where

      Pn2​δ\displaystyle{P}_{n^{2\delta}} =∑m=0n2​δ|m⟩​⟨m|.\displaystyle=\sum_{m=0}^{n^{2\delta}}|m\rangle\langle m|. (12)

      The output state on the first mode is encoded in a quantum memory.

  • •

    Decoder.

    1. 1.

      First read α^∗\hat{\alpha}^{\ast} and perform the displacement operation 𝒟n−n1−δ​α^∗\mathcal{D}_{\sqrt{n-n^{1-\delta}}\hat{\alpha}^{\ast}} on the state of the quantum memory.

    2. 2.

      To recover the distortion caused by the estimation of α\alpha, a quantum amplifier [21] 𝒜γn\mathcal{A}^{\gamma_{n}} with γn=1/(1−n−δ)\gamma_{n}=1/(1-n^{-\delta}) is applied to the output state. A quantum amplifier is a device that increases the intensity of quantum light while preserving its phase information, defined by the following quantum channel

      𝒜γ​(ρ)\displaystyle\mathcal{A}^{\gamma}(\rho) =TrB[ecosh−1⁡(γ)​(a†​b†−a​b)​(ρ⊗|0⟩​⟨0|B)​ecosh−1⁡(γ)​(a​b−a†​b†)]\displaystyle=\mathop{\rm Tr}\nolimits_{B}\left[e^{\cosh^{-1}(\sqrt{\gamma})(a^{\dagger}b^{\dagger}-ab)}(\rho\otimes|0\rangle\langle 0|_{B})e^{\cosh^{-1}(\sqrt{\gamma})(ab-a^{\dagger}b^{\dagger})}\right] (13)

      where aa and bb are the annihilation operators of the input mode and the ancillary mode BB, respectively.

    3. 3.

      Prepare the other (n−1)(n-1) modes in the thermal state ρβ(thm)\rho^{({\rm thm})}_{\beta}.

    4. 4.

      Perform on all the nn modes the inverse of the unitary channel 𝒰BS\mathcal{U}_{\rm BS}

      𝒰BS−1​(ρ)=UBS†​ρ​UBS.\displaystyle\mathcal{U}_{\rm BS}^{-1}(\rho)=U^{\dagger}_{\rm BS}\,\rho\,U_{\rm BS}. (14)

The memory cost consists of two parts: the cost of encoding the (rounded) value α^∗\hat{\alpha}^{\ast} of the estimate which is log⁡n\log n bits and the cost of encoding the first mode (in a displaced thermal state) which is 2​δ​log⁡n2\delta\log n qubits. Overall, the protocol requires 2​δ​log⁡n2\delta\log n qubits and log⁡n\log n classical bits.

On the other hand, the error of the protocol can be split into three terms as

ϵ\displaystyle\epsilon ≤∫|α^−α|>n−1/2+3δ/4Q(dα^|α)\displaystyle\leq\int_{|\hat{\alpha}-\alpha|>n^{-1/2+3\delta/4}}Q(\mathop{\rm d}\nolimits\hat{\alpha}|\alpha)
+12supα,βsupα^∗:|α^∗−α|≤n−1/2+3δ/4{‖𝒜γn(ρn−n1−δ​α,β)−ρn​α,β‖1+‖𝒫n2​δ(ρn−n1−δ​(α−α^∗),β)−ρn−n1−δ​(α−α^∗),β‖1}.\displaystyle\qquad+\frac{1}{2}\sup_{\alpha,\beta}\sup_{\hat{\alpha}^{\ast}:|\hat{\alpha}^{\ast}-\alpha|\leq n^{-1/2+3\delta/4}}\left\{\left\|\mathcal{A}^{\gamma_{n}}(\rho_{\sqrt{n-n^{1-\delta}}\alpha,\beta})-\rho_{\sqrt{n}\alpha,\beta}\right\|_{1}+\left\|\mathcal{P}_{n^{2\delta}}(\rho_{\sqrt{n-n^{1-\delta}}(\alpha-\hat{\alpha}^{\ast}),\beta})-\rho_{\sqrt{n-n^{1-\delta}}(\alpha-\hat{\alpha}^{\ast}),\beta}\right\|_{1}\right\}.

Now we bound them one by one. First, from Eq. (10) we get

∫|α^−α|>n−1/2+3δ/4Q(dα^|α)\displaystyle\int_{|\hat{\alpha}-\alpha|>n^{-1/2+3\delta/4}}Q(\mathop{\rm d}\nolimits\hat{\alpha}|\alpha) =∫|α^−α|>n−1/2+3δ/4(1−β)exp[−(1−β)n1−δ|α^−α|2]=e−Ω⁡(nδ/2).\displaystyle=\int_{|\hat{\alpha}-\alpha|>n^{-1/2+3\delta/4}}(1-\beta)\exp[-(1-\beta)n^{1-\delta}|\hat{\alpha}-\alpha|^{2}]=e^{-\Omega(n^{\delta/2})}.

Second, explicit calculation shows that, when the input state is a displaced thermal state ρα,β\rho_{\alpha,\beta}, the output state of the amplifier is

𝒜γ​(ρα,β)=ρα,β′β′=β​γ+4​(1−β)​γ​(γ−1)γ+(1−β)​(γ−1).\displaystyle\mathcal{A}^{\gamma}\left(\rho_{\alpha,\beta}\right)=\rho_{\alpha,\beta^{\prime}}\qquad\beta^{\prime}=\frac{\beta\gamma+4(1-\beta)\gamma(\gamma-1)}{\gamma+(1-\beta)(\gamma-1)}. (15)

We thus have

12supα,βsupα^∗:|α^∗−α|≤n−1/2+3δ/4‖𝒜γn(ρn−n1−δ​α,β)−ρn​α,β‖1\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\sup_{\alpha,\beta}\sup_{\hat{\alpha}^{\ast}:|\hat{\alpha}^{\ast}-\alpha|\leq n^{-1/2+3\delta/4}}\left\|\mathcal{A}^{\gamma_{n}}(\rho_{\sqrt{n-n^{1-\delta}}\alpha,\beta})-\rho_{\sqrt{n}\alpha,\beta}\right\|_{1} =O⁡(n−δ)\displaystyle=O(n^{-\delta})

having used Eq. (19). Finally, the error of 𝒫n2​δ\mathcal{P}_{n^{2\delta}} can be bounded using the following lemma, whose proof can be found in Appendix.

Lemma 2 (Photon number truncation of displaced thermal states.).

Define the channel 𝒫N\mathcal{P}_{N} as

𝒫N​(ρ)=PN​ρ​PN+(1−Tr[PN​ρ])​|0⟩​⟨0|\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{N}(\rho)=P_{N}\rho P_{N}+(1-\mathop{\rm Tr}\nolimits[P_{N}\rho])|0\rangle\langle 0| (16)

where

PN=∑k=0N|k⟩​⟨k|.\displaystyle P_{N}=\sum_{k=0}^{N}|k\rangle\langle k|. (17)

When N=Ω⁡(|α|2+x)N=\Omega\left(|\alpha|^{2+x}\right), 𝒫N\mathcal{P}_{N} satisfies

ϵ⁡(ρα,β)=12​‖𝒫N​(ρα,β)−ρα,β‖1=βΩ⁡(Nx/8)+e−Ω⁡(Nx/4)\displaystyle\epsilon(\rho_{\alpha,\beta})=\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathcal{P}_{N}\left(\rho_{\alpha,\beta}\right)-\rho_{\alpha,\beta}\right\|_{1}=\beta^{\Omega(N^{x/8})}+e^{-\Omega(N^{x/4})} (18)

for any 0≤β<10\leq\beta<1.

In our case we are using the projector Pn2​δP_{n^{2\delta}} in Eq. (12), and the displacement is n−n1−δ​(α−α^∗)\sqrt{n-n^{1-\delta}}(\alpha-\hat{\alpha}^{\ast}). Since (n−n1−δ)​|α−α^∗|2=O⁡(n3​δ/2)(n-n^{1-\delta})|\alpha-\hat{\alpha}^{\ast}|^{2}=O\left(n^{3\delta/2}\right), by Lemma 2 we obtain the bound

12supα,βsupα^∗:|α^∗−α|≤n−1/2+3δ/4‖𝒫n2​δ(ρn−n1−δ​(α−α^∗),β)−ρn−n1−δ​(α−α^∗),β‖1\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\sup_{\alpha,\beta}\sup_{\hat{\alpha}^{\ast}:|\hat{\alpha}^{\ast}-\alpha|\leq n^{-1/2+3\delta/4}}\left\|\mathcal{P}_{n^{2\delta}}(\rho_{\sqrt{n-n^{1-\delta}}(\alpha-\hat{\alpha}^{\ast}),\beta})-\rho_{\sqrt{n-n^{1-\delta}}(\alpha-\hat{\alpha}^{\ast}),\beta}\right\|_{1} =βΩ⁡(nδ/12)+e−Ω⁡(nδ/6)\displaystyle=\beta^{\Omega\left(n^{\delta/12}\right)}+e^{-\Omega(n^{\delta/6})}

Summarizing the above bounds for each term of the error, we get

ϵ\displaystyle\epsilon =O⁡(n−δ).\displaystyle=O\left(n^{-\delta}\right)\,.

III-C Case 3: unknown α\alpha, unknown β\beta.

Case 3 can be treated in a similar way as Case 2, except that we also have to estimate and encode β\beta. Luckily, unlike α\alpha, the thermal parameter β\beta can be estimated freely (i.e. without distortion of the input state), and thus its estimation strategy is simpler.

In detail, for any δ>0\delta>0 we can then construct the protocol for displaced thermal states with unknown β\beta and unknown α\alpha as follows:

  • •

    Preprocessing. Divide the range of α\alpha into nn zones, each labeled by a point α^i\hat{\alpha}_{i} in it, so that |α′−α′′|=O(n−1/2)|\alpha^{\prime}-\alpha^{\prime\prime}|=O(n^{-1/2}) for any α′,α′′\alpha^{\prime},\alpha^{\prime\prime} in the same zone.

  • •

    Encoder.

    1. 1.

      First perform the unitary channel 𝒰BS​(⋅)=UBS⋅UBS†\mathcal{U}_{\rm BS}(\cdot)=U_{\rm BS}\,\cdot\,U_{\rm BS}^{\dagger} on the input state, where UBSU_{\rm BS} is the unitary defined by Eq. (8). The output state has the form ρn​α,β⊗(ρβ(thm))⊗(n−1)\rho_{\sqrt{n}\alpha,\beta}\otimes\left(\rho^{({\rm thm})}_{\beta}\right)^{\otimes(n-1)}.

    2. 2.

      Estimate β\beta with the von Neumann measurement of the photon number on the n−1n-1 copies of ρβ(thm)\rho^{({\rm thm})}_{\beta} and denote by β^\hat{\beta} the maximum likelihood estimate of β\beta. Note that these copies will not be disturbed since they are diagonal in the photon number basis.

    3. 3.

      Next, send the first and the last mode through a beam splitter with transitivity n−δn^{-\delta}. The nn-mode state is now ρn−n1−δ​α,β⊗(ρβ(thm))⊗(n−2)⊗ρn1−δ​α,β\rho_{\sqrt{n-n^{1-\delta}}\alpha,\beta}\otimes\left(\rho^{({\rm thm})}_{\beta}\right)^{\otimes(n-2)}\otimes\rho_{\sqrt{n^{1-\delta}}\alpha,\beta}.

    4. 4.

      Estimate α\alpha by the heterodyne measurement {d2α′​|α′⟩​⟨α′|}\{\mathop{\rm d}\nolimits^{2}\alpha^{\prime}|\alpha^{\prime}\rangle\langle\alpha^{\prime}|\} on the last mode, which yields an estimate α^=α′/n1−δ\hat{\alpha}=\alpha^{\prime}/\sqrt{n^{1-\delta}} with the probability distribution Q⁡(α^|α)Q(\hat{\alpha}|\alpha) (10). Encode the label of the zone α^∗\hat{\alpha}^{\ast} containing α^\hat{\alpha} in a classical memory.

    5. 5.

      Displace the first mode with 𝒟−n−n1−δ​α^∗\mathcal{D}_{-\sqrt{n-n^{1-\delta}}\hat{\alpha}^{\ast}}.

    6. 6.

      Prepare the nn-th mode in the thermal state ρβ^(thm)\rho^{({\rm thm})}_{\hat{\beta}}. The nn-mode state is now ρn−n1−δ​(α−α^∗),β⊗(ρβ(thm))⊗(n−2)⊗ρβ^(thm)\rho_{\sqrt{n-n^{1-\delta}}(\alpha-\hat{\alpha}^{\ast}),\beta}\otimes\left(\rho^{({\rm thm})}_{\beta}\right)^{\otimes(n-2)}\otimes\rho^{({\rm thm})}_{\hat{\beta}}.

    7. 7.

      The state of the first mode then goes through a truncation in the photon number basis, described by the channel 𝒫n2​δ\mathcal{P}_{n^{2\delta}} defined by Eq. (16). The output state on the first mode is encoded in a quantum memory.

    8. 8.

      Meanwhile, use the thermal state encoder ℰn−1,δ(thm)\mathcal{E}^{({\rm thm})}_{n-1,\delta} (see Lemma 1) to compress the remaining n−1n-1 modes and encode the output state in a classical memory.

  • •

    Decoder.

    1. 1.

      First read α^∗\hat{\alpha}^{\ast} and perform the displacement 𝒟n−n1−δ​α^∗\mathcal{D}_{\sqrt{n-n^{1-\delta}}\hat{\alpha}^{\ast}} on the state of the quantum memory.

    2. 2.

      Apply a quantum amplifier 𝒜γn\mathcal{A}^{\gamma_{n}} with γn=1/(1−n−δ)\gamma_{n}=1/(1-n^{-\delta}) to the state.

    3. 3.

      Then use the thermal state decoder 𝒟n−1,δ(thm)\mathcal{D}^{({\rm thm})}_{n-1,\delta} to recover the other (n−1)(n-1) modes in the thermal state ρβ(thm)\rho^{({\rm thm})}_{\beta} from the memory.

    4. 4.

      Finally, perform the inverse of the unitary channel 𝒰BS\mathcal{U}_{\rm BS}.

The memory cost consists of three parts: the cost of encoding the (rounded) value α^∗\hat{\alpha}^{\ast} of the estimate which is log⁡n\log n bits, the cost of encoding the first mode (displaced thermal state) which is 2​δ​log⁡n2\delta\log n qubits, and the cost of encoding the other modes (thermal states) which is (1/2+δ)​log⁡n(1/2+\delta)\log n bits. Overall, the protocol requires 2​δ​log⁡n2\delta\log n qubits and (3/2+δ)​log⁡n(3/2+\delta)\log n classical bits.

On the other hand, the error of the protocol can be split into several terms as

ϵ\displaystyle\epsilon ≤12​supβ‖𝒟n,δ(thm)∘ℰn,δ(thm)​[∫dβ^​P​(dβ^|β)​ρβ^(thm)⊗(ρβ(thm))⊗(n−1)]−(ρβ(thm))⊗n‖1\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\sup_{\beta}\left\|\mathcal{D}^{({\rm thm})}_{n,\delta}\circ\mathcal{E}^{({\rm thm})}_{n,\delta}\left[\int\mathop{\rm d}\nolimits\hat{\beta}\,P(\mathop{\rm d}\nolimits\hat{\beta}|\beta)\,\rho^{({\rm thm})}_{\hat{\beta}}\otimes\left(\rho^{({\rm thm})}_{\beta}\right)^{\otimes(n-1)}\right]-\left(\rho^{({\rm thm})}_{\beta}\right)^{\otimes n}\right\|_{1}
+12supα,βsupα^∗:|α^∗−α|≤n−1/2+3δ/4{‖𝒫N(num)(ρn−n1−δ​(α−α^∗),β)−ρn−n1−δ​(α−α^∗),β‖1+‖𝒜γn(ρn−n1−δ​α,β)−ρn​α,β‖1}\displaystyle\qquad+\frac{1}{2}\sup_{\alpha,\beta}\sup_{\hat{\alpha}^{\ast}:|\hat{\alpha}^{\ast}-\alpha|\leq n^{-1/2+3\delta/4}}\left\{\left\|\mathcal{P}^{({\rm num})}_{N}(\rho_{\sqrt{n-n^{1-\delta}}(\alpha-\hat{\alpha}^{\ast}),\beta})-\rho_{\sqrt{n-n^{1-\delta}}(\alpha-\hat{\alpha}^{\ast}),\beta}\right\|_{1}+\left\|\mathcal{A}^{\gamma_{n}}(\rho_{\sqrt{n-n^{1-\delta}}\alpha,\beta})-\rho_{\sqrt{n}\alpha,\beta}\right\|_{1}\right\}
+∫|α^−α|>n−1/2+3δ/4Q(dα^|α)\displaystyle\qquad\quad+\int_{|\hat{\alpha}-\alpha|>n^{-1/2+3\delta/4}}Q(\mathop{\rm d}\nolimits\hat{\alpha}|\alpha)

where P⁡(dβ^|β)P(\mathop{\rm d}\nolimits\hat{\beta}|\beta) denotes the probability distribution of the estimate for the input value β\beta. The latter three terms are the errors of estimation and compression of the displaced thermal state ρn​α,β\rho_{\sqrt{n}\alpha,\beta} of the first mode, which have been bounded in the previous subsection as O⁡(n−δ)O(n^{-\delta}). We now bound the first term ϵβ\epsilon_{\beta}, which is the error of compressing and estimating thermal states. ϵβ\epsilon_{\beta} can be further split into two terms as

ϵβ\displaystyle\epsilon_{\beta} ≤12​supβ{‖𝒟n,δ(thm)∘ℰn,δ(thm)​[(ρβ(thm))⊗n]−(ρβ(thm))⊗n‖1+‖∫P⁡(dβ^|β)​ρβ^(thm)−ρβ(thm)‖1}.\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\sup_{\beta}\left\{\left\|\mathcal{D}^{({\rm thm})}_{n,\delta}\circ\mathcal{E}^{({\rm thm})}_{n,\delta}\left[\left(\rho^{({\rm thm})}_{\beta}\right)^{\otimes n}\right]-\left(\rho^{({\rm thm})}_{\beta}\right)^{\otimes n}\right\|_{1}+\left\|\int\,P(\mathop{\rm d}\nolimits\hat{\beta}|\beta)\,\rho^{({\rm thm})}_{\hat{\beta}}-\rho^{({\rm thm})}_{\beta}\right\|_{1}\right\}.

On the right hand side of the inequality, the first error term is bounded by Lemma 1, while the second error term is bounded by the following property of the maximum likelihood estimate [22]

∫|β^−β|≥l/n​FβP⁡(dβ^|β)≤erfc⁡(l2)\displaystyle\int_{|\hat{\beta}-\beta|\geq l/\sqrt{nF_{\beta}}}\,P(\mathop{\rm d}\nolimits\hat{\beta}|\beta)\leq\erfc\left(\frac{l}{\sqrt{2}}\right)

where Fβ=(β2+1)/[β​(1−β)3]F_{\beta}=(\beta^{2}+1)/[\beta(1-\beta)^{3}] is the Fisher information of β\beta and erfc⁡(x):=(2/π)​∫x∞e−s2​ds\erfc(x):=(2/\pi)\int_{x}^{\infty}e^{-s^{2}}\mathop{\rm d}\nolimits s is the complementary error function. ϵβ\epsilon_{\beta} can thus be bounded as

ϵβ\displaystyle\epsilon_{\beta} ≤O(n−δ)+12supβsupβ^:|β^−β|≤n−(1+δ)/2‖ρβ^(thm)−ρβ(thm)‖1+e−Ω⁡(nδ)\displaystyle\leq O(n^{-\delta})+\frac{1}{2}\sup_{\beta}\sup_{\hat{\beta}:|\hat{\beta}-\beta|\leq n^{-(1+\delta)/2}}\left\|\rho^{({\rm thm})}_{\hat{\beta}}-\rho^{({\rm thm})}_{\beta}\right\|_{1}+e^{-\Omega(n^{\delta})}
=O⁡(n−δ)\displaystyle=O(n^{-\delta})

having used the tail property of complementary error function and the property

‖ρα(thm)−ρβ(thm)‖1\displaystyle\left\|\rho^{({\rm thm})}_{\alpha}-\rho^{({\rm thm})}_{\beta}\right\|_{1} =2​|α−β|(1−α)2+O⁡(|α−β|2).\displaystyle=\frac{2|\alpha-\beta|}{(1-\alpha)^{2}}+O(|\alpha-\beta|^{2}). (19)

Summarizing the above bounds for each term of the error, we get

ϵ\displaystyle\epsilon =O⁡(n−δ).\displaystyle=O\left(n^{-\delta}\right)\,.

III-D Case 4: fixed |α||\alpha|, free TT, fixed β\beta and Case 6: free |α||\alpha|, fixed TT, fixed β\beta.

In Case 4 and Case 6, the displacement α\alpha is partially known. Such a knowledge allows us to reduce the amount of memory. Since the protocols for these two cases are very similar. The protocol for Case 4 runs as in the following:

  • •

    Preprocessing. Divide the range of TT into n−1/2n^{-1/2} zones, each labeled by a point T^i\hat{T}_{i} in it, so that |T′−T′′|=O(n−1/2)|T^{\prime}-T^{\prime\prime}|=O(n^{-1/2}) for any T′,T′′T^{\prime},T^{\prime\prime} in the same zone.

  • •

    Encoder.

    1. 1.

      First perform the unitary channel 𝒰BS​(⋅)\mathcal{U}_{\rm BS}(\cdot) on the input state to transform it into ρn​α,β⊗(ρβ(thm))⊗(n−1)\rho_{\sqrt{n}\alpha,\beta}\otimes\left(\rho^{({\rm thm})}_{\beta}\right)^{\otimes(n-1)}.

    2. 2.

      Next, send the first and the last mode through a beam splitter with transitivity n−δ/2n^{-\delta/2}. The nn-mode state is now ρn−n1−δ/2​α,β⊗(ρβ(thm))⊗(n−2)⊗ρn1−δ/2​α,β\rho_{\sqrt{n-n^{1-\delta/2}}\alpha,\beta}\otimes\left(\rho^{({\rm thm})}_{\beta}\right)^{\otimes(n-2)}\otimes\rho_{\sqrt{n^{1-\delta/2}}\alpha,\beta}.

    3. 3.

      Estimate TT by the heterodyne measurement d2α′​|α′⟩​⟨α′|\mathop{\rm d}\nolimits^{2}\alpha^{\prime}|\alpha^{\prime}\rangle\langle\alpha^{\prime}| on the last mode, which yields an estimate T^\hat{T} which is the phase of α′\alpha^{\prime}. Encode the label of the zone T^∗\hat{T}^{\ast} containing T^\hat{T} in a classical memory.

    4. 4.

      Displace the first mode with 𝒟−n−n1−δ/2​α^∗\mathcal{D}_{-\sqrt{n-n^{1-\delta/2}}\hat{\alpha}^{\ast}} with α^∗:=|α|​ei​T^∗\hat{\alpha}^{\ast}:=|\alpha|e^{i\hat{T}^{\ast}}.

    5. 5.

      Then send the state of the first mode through a truncation channel 𝒫nδ\mathcal{P}_{n^{\delta}} defined in (16) and encode the output state in a quantum memory.

  • •

    Decoder.

    1. 1.

      First read α^∗\hat{\alpha}^{\ast} and perform the displacement 𝒟n−n1−δ/2​α^∗\mathcal{D}_{\sqrt{n-n^{1-\delta/2}}\hat{\alpha}^{\ast}} on the state of the quantum memory.

    2. 2.

      Then apply the quantum amplifier 𝒜γn\mathcal{A}^{\gamma_{n}} with γn=1/(1−n−δ/2)\gamma_{n}=1/(1-n^{-\delta/2}).

    3. 3.

      Prepare the other (n−1)(n-1) modes in the thermal state ρβ(thm)\rho^{({\rm thm})}_{\beta}.

    4. 4.

      Finally, perform 𝒰BS−1\mathcal{U}^{-1}_{\rm BS} on the output of 𝒟n−1(thm)\mathcal{D}^{({\rm thm})}_{n-1} and the quantum memory.

The protocol for Case 6 works in the same way except that |α||\alpha| is estimated instead of TT. For both cases the memory cost consists of three parts: the cost of encoding the (rounded) value α^∗\hat{\alpha}^{\ast} of the estimate which is (1/2)​log⁡n(1/2)\log n bits, the cost of encoding the first mode (displaced thermal state) which is δ​log⁡n\delta\log n qubits, and the cost of encoding the other modes (thermal states) which is (1/2+δ)​log⁡n(1/2+\delta)\log n bits. Overall, the protocol requires δ​log⁡n\delta\log n qubits and (1+2​δ)​log⁡n(1+2\delta)\log n classical bits. The error can be bounded as previous as

ϵ\displaystyle\epsilon =O(n−δ/2).\displaystyle=O\left(n^{-\delta/2}\right)\,.

Case 5 and Case 7 can be treated in the same way as Case 4 and Case 6, adding additional steps to estimate and encode β\beta. The protocol for Case 5 runs as follows:

IV Compression of identically prepared finite dimensional systems.

In this section, we study the compression of d(<∞)d(<\infty)-dimensional non-degenerate quantum systems, based on the results on displaced thermal states and quantum local asymptotic normality. We show that, just as for displaced thermal states, each free parameter of a qudit subfamily requires (1/2+δ)​log⁡n(1/2+\delta)\log n memory for any δ>0\delta>0. Details of the compression protocol are introduced in the following.

IV-A The compression protocol

To construct a compression protocol, we need the following techniques:

  • •

    Quantum local asymptotic normality (Q-LAN). The quantum version of local asymptotic normality has been derived in several different contexts [16, 17, 18]. Here we use the result of [18], which states that nn identical copies of a qudit state can be approximated by a classical-quantum Gaussian state in a sufficiently small neighborhood of a point θ0∈Θ\theta_{0}\in\mathsf{\Theta} for large nn. Explicitly, for a fixed point θ0=(μ0,ξ0)\theta_{0}=\left(\mu_{0},\xi_{0}\right) and for a fixed x∈(0,1)x\in(0,1), we define the following neighborhood

    Θn,x(θ0)={θ=θ0+δθ/n,|∥δθ∥∞≤nx2},\displaystyle\mathsf{\Theta}_{n,x}(\theta_{0})=\left\{\theta=\theta_{0}+\delta\theta/\sqrt{n},~|~\|\delta\theta\|_{\infty}\leq n^{\frac{x}{2}}\right\}\,, (20)

    where ‖δ​θ‖∞\|\delta\theta\|_{\infty} is the max vector norm defined as ‖δ​θ‖∞:=maxi⁡(δ​θ)i\|\delta\theta\|_{\infty}:=\max_{i}(\delta\theta)_{i}. Q-LAN states that every nn-fold product state ρθ⊗n\rho_{\theta}^{\otimes n} with θ\theta in the neighborhood Θn,x​(θ0)\mathsf{\Theta}_{n,x}(\theta_{0}) can be approximated by a classical-quantum Gaussian state. Specifically, the stated ρθ⊗n\rho_{\theta}^{\otimes n} is approximated by the Gaussian state

    Gn,θ\displaystyle G_{n,\theta} =Nδ​μ,Iμ0​⨂j<kραj,k,βj,k,\displaystyle=N_{\delta\mu,I_{\mu_{0}}}\,\bigotimes_{j<k}\rho_{\alpha_{j,k},\beta_{j,k}}, (21)

    where Nδ​μ,Iμ0N_{\delta\mu,I_{\mu_{0}}} is the multivariate normal distribution with mean δ​μ\delta\mu and covariance matrix Iμ0I_{\mu_{0}} (equal to the inverse of the quantum Fisher information of the eigenvalues μ\mu, evaluated at μ0\mu_{0}) and ραj,k,βj,k\rho_{\alpha_{j,k},\beta_{j,k}} is the displaced thermal state defined as

    ραj,k,βj,k\displaystyle\rho_{\alpha_{j,k},\beta_{j,k}} =Dαj,k​ρβj,k(thm)​Dαj,k†\displaystyle=D_{\alpha_{j,k}}\rho^{({\rm thm})}_{\beta_{j,k}}D^{\dagger}_{\alpha_{j,k}} (22)
    αj,k\displaystyle\alpha_{j,k} =δ​ξj,kR+i​δ​ξj,kI2​(μ0)j−(μ0)kβj,k=(μ0)k(μ0)j.\displaystyle=\frac{\delta\xi^{R}_{j,k}+i\delta\xi^{I}_{j,k}}{2\sqrt{(\mu_{0})_{j}-(\mu_{0})_{k}}}\qquad\beta_{j,k}=\frac{(\mu_{0})_{k}}{(\mu_{0})_{j}}. (23)

    where (μ0)j(\mu_{0})_{j} and (μ0)k(\mu_{0})_{k} are components of μ0\mu_{0}. The approximation is physically implemented by two quantum channels 𝒯θ0(n)\mathcal{T}_{\theta_{0}}^{(n)} and 𝒮θ0(n)\mathcal{S}_{\theta_{0}}^{(n)}, satisfying the conditions

    supθ∈Θn,x​(θ0,c)‖𝒯θ0(n)​(ρθ⊗n)−Gn,θ‖1=O⁡(n−κ⁡(x))\displaystyle\sup_{\theta\in\mathsf{\Theta}_{n,x}(\theta_{0},c)}\left\|\mathcal{T}_{\theta_{0}}^{(n)}\left(\rho_{\theta}^{\otimes n}\right)-G_{n,\theta}\right\|_{1}=O\left(n^{-\kappa(x)}\right) (24)
    supθ∈Θn,x​(θ0,c)‖ρθ⊗n−𝒮θ0(n)​(Gn,θ)‖1=O⁡(n−κ⁡(x)),\displaystyle\sup_{\theta\in\mathsf{\Theta}_{n,x}(\theta_{0},c)}\left\|\rho_{\theta}^{\otimes n}-\mathcal{S}^{(n)}_{\theta_{0}}\left(G_{n,\theta}\right)\right\|_{1}=O\left(n^{-\kappa(x)}\right), (25)

    where ∥⋅∥1\|\cdot\|_{1} denotes the trace norm and

    κ⁡(x)=min⁡{1−z−η2,1−x−2​y2−y,2−9​η24}\displaystyle\kappa(x)=\min\left\{\frac{1-z-\eta}{2},\frac{1-x-2y}{2}-y,\frac{2-9\eta}{24}\right\} (26)

    under the constraints 1>z>1+x/21>z>1+x/2, y>0y>0, η>0\eta>0 and η>x−y\eta>x-y. We note that κ⁡(x)>0\kappa(x)>0 when x∈[0,2/9)x\in[0,2/9).

  • •

    Quantum state tomography. State tomography is an important technique of quantum information processing which is used to determine the density matrix of an unknown quantum state. The role of tomography here is to provide a rough estimate of θ0\theta_{0} so that we can apply Q-LAN. The tomography protocol used here [23] gives an estimate ρθ^\rho_{\hat{\theta}} of a qudit state ρθ\rho_{\theta} with confidence

    𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐛[12∥ρθ−ρθ^∥1≤ϵ]≥1−(n+1)3​d2e−n​ϵ2\displaystyle\mathbf{Prob}\left[\frac{1}{2}\|\rho_{\theta}-\rho_{\hat{\theta}}\|_{1}\leq\epsilon\right]\geq 1-(n+1)^{3d^{2}}e^{-n\epsilon^{2}} (27)

    using nn copies of the state.

For any δ∈(0,2/9)\delta\in(0,2/9), our compression protocol runs as follows:

  • •

    Encode the input state into memories. We break the encoding of ρθ⊗n\rho_{\theta}^{\otimes n} into four steps:

    1. 1.

      Tomography. First take out n1−δ/2n^{1-\delta/2} copies of ρθ\rho_{\theta} for quantum tomography. In this way, one obtains a neighborhood Θn,2​δ/3​(θ0)\mathsf{\Theta}_{n,2\delta/3}(\theta_{0}) (note that 2​δ/32\delta/3 is not the only choice) that contains the state with confidence approaching one in the large nn limit. To encode the outcome of the tomography, the parameter space Θ\mathsf{\Theta} is discretized into a lattice of n(fc+fq)/2n^{(f_{c}+f_{q})/2} points, each point corresponding to an outcome of tomography. The point that is closest to θ0\theta_{0} is encoded in a classical memory.

    2. 2.

      Q-LAN. After the tomography step, n−n1−δ/2n-n^{1-\delta/2} copies remain for compression. Define

      γn=1/(1−n−δ/2).\displaystyle\gamma_{n}=1/(1-n^{-\delta/2}). (28)

      so that the number of remaining copies is n/γnn/\gamma_{n}. The n/γnn/\gamma_{n} copies are sent through the channel 𝒯θ0(n/γn)\mathcal{T}_{\theta_{0}}^{(n/\gamma_{n})} (24) which outputs the Gaussian state G(n/γn),θG_{(n/\gamma_{n}),\theta} defined by Eq. (21).

    3. 3.

      Amplification. Next, the Gaussian state is amplified to compensate the loss of input copies. The state ραj,k,βj,k\rho_{\alpha_{j,k},\beta_{j,k}} of each quantum mode is amplified by 𝒜γn\mathcal{A}^{\gamma_{n}}. The Gaussian distribution on the classical register is rescaled by a constant factor:

      |u⟩→|γn​u⟩,|u\rangle\to|\sqrt{\gamma_{n}}u\rangle,

      where {|u⟩}\{|u\rangle\} stands for the Cartesian basis of the classical register. The whole amplification progress is described by the channel 𝒜θ0(n/γn)→n\mathcal{A}^{(n/\gamma_{n})\to n}_{\theta_{0}}, whose action on any product state is

      𝒜θ0(n/γn)→n​(ρ⊗j<kσj,k)=∑u⟨u|ρ⁡|u⟩|γn​u⟩​⟨γn​u|​⨂j<k𝒜γn​(σj,k).\displaystyle\mathcal{A}^{(n/\gamma_{n})\to n}_{\theta_{0}}\left(\rho\otimes_{j<k}\sigma_{j,k}\right)=\sum_{u}\langle u|\rho|u\rangle|\sqrt{\gamma_{n}}u\rangle\langle\sqrt{\gamma_{n}}u|\bigotimes_{j<k}\mathcal{A}^{\gamma_{n}}(\sigma_{j,k}). (29)

      where uu is summed over the basis of the classical register.

    4. 4.

      Gaussian state compression. Each quantum mode of the amplified Gaussian state is then truncated by 𝒫nδ\mathcal{P}_{n^{\delta}} (16). The output state is then stored in a quantum memory. The state of the classical mode is compressed by an channel 𝒫c\mathcal{P}_{c} that truncates the state into a O⁡(nδ)O(n^{\delta})-hypercube centered around the mean of the Gaussian. Explicitly, we have

      𝒫c​(ρ)\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{\rm c}(\rho) =∑‖u‖∞≤nδ⟨u|ρ⁡|u⟩|u⟩​⟨u​|+[1−∑‖u′‖∞≤nδ⟨u′|ρ|u′⟩]|​0⟩​⟨0|.\displaystyle=\sum_{\|u\|_{\infty}\leq n^{\delta}}\langle u|\rho|u\rangle\,|u\rangle\langle u|+\left[1-\sum_{\|u^{\prime}\|_{\infty}\leq n^{\delta}}\langle u^{\prime}|\rho|u^{\prime}\rangle\right]|0\rangle\langle 0|. (30)

      The whole process is described by the channel

      𝒫θ0(n)\displaystyle\mathcal{P}^{(n)}_{\theta_{0}} =𝒫c​⨂j<k𝒫nδ.\displaystyle=\mathcal{P}_{\rm c}\bigotimes_{j<k}\mathcal{P}_{n^{\delta}}\,. (31)
  • •

    Recover the original state. The state can be decompressed from the memory by sending the state of the hybrid memory through the channel 𝒮θ0(n)\mathcal{S}_{\theta_{0}}^{(n)} (25), which can be constructed by consulting the outcome of tomography.

IV-B Error analysis.

Here we bound the error of the protocol. Using the triangle inequality of trace distance, we split the overall error into four terms

ϵ≤\displaystyle\epsilon\leq ϵtomo+ϵamp+ϵG+ϵLAN,\displaystyle\epsilon_{\rm tomo}+\epsilon_{\rm amp}+\epsilon_{\rm G}+\epsilon_{\rm LAN}, (32)

where

ϵtomo\displaystyle\epsilon_{\rm tomo} =𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐛[θ∉Θn,2​δ/3(θ0)]\displaystyle=\mathbf{Prob}\left[\theta\not\in\mathsf{\Theta}_{n,2\delta/3}(\theta_{0})\right] (33)
ϵamp\displaystyle\epsilon_{\rm amp} =12​supθ0supθ∈Θn,2​δ/3​(θ0)‖𝒜θ0(n/γn)→n​(Gn/γn,θ)−Gn,θ‖1\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sup_{\theta_{0}}\sup_{\theta\in\mathsf{\Theta}_{n,2\delta/3}(\theta_{0})}\left\|\mathcal{A}^{(n/\gamma_{n})\to n}_{\theta_{0}}\left(G_{n/\gamma_{n},\theta}\right)-G_{n,\theta}\right\|_{1} (34)
ϵG\displaystyle\epsilon_{\rm G} =12​supθ0supθ∈Θn,2​δ/3​(θ0)‖𝒫θ0(n)​(Gn,θ)−Gn,θ‖1\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sup_{\theta_{0}}\sup_{\theta\in\mathsf{\Theta}_{n,2\delta/3}(\theta_{0})}\left\|\mathcal{P}^{(n)}_{\theta_{0}}\left(G_{n,\theta}\right)-G_{n,\theta}\right\|_{1} (35)
ϵQ−LAN\displaystyle\epsilon_{\rm Q-LAN} =12​supθ0supθ∈Θn,2​δ/3​(θ0){‖𝒯θ0(n/γn)​(ρθ⊗(n/γn))−Gn/γn,θ‖1+‖ρθ⊗n−𝒮θ0(n)​(Gn,θ)‖1}\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sup_{\theta_{0}}\sup_{\theta\in\mathsf{\Theta}_{n,2\delta/3}(\theta_{0})}\left\{\left\|\mathcal{T}^{(n/\gamma_{n})}_{\theta_{0}}\left(\rho_{\theta}^{\otimes(n/\gamma_{n})}\right)-G_{n/\gamma_{n},\theta}\right\|_{1}+\left\|\rho_{\theta}^{\otimes n}-\mathcal{S}^{(n)}_{\theta_{0}}\left(G_{n,\theta}\right)\right\|_{1}\right\} (36)

are the error terms of tomography, amplification, truncation, and Q-LAN, respectively.

We first briefly review the process of tomography and then bound its error. Using n1−δ/2n^{1-\delta/2} copies of ρθ\rho_{\theta}, an estimate θ^\hat{\theta} of θ\theta is obtained. The estimate θ^\hat{\theta} is then encoded as a point in the lattice 𝖫:={θ∈Θ||θi|=zi/(2n),zi∈ℕ∀i}\mathsf{L}:=\{\theta\in\mathsf{\Theta}~|~|\theta_{i}|=z_{i}/(2\sqrt{n}),z_{i}\in\mathbb{N}\ \forall\ i\}. Naturally, we encode the coordinate of the lattice point θ0\theta_{0} that is closest to θ^\hat{\theta}. Namely that we choose

θ0:=argminθ′∈𝖫‖θ^−θ′‖∞.\displaystyle\theta_{0}:=\mathop{\rm argmin}_{\theta^{\prime}\in\mathsf{L}}\|\hat{\theta}-\theta^{\prime}\|_{\infty}. (37)

Recall that ‖θ‖∞:=maxi⁡(θ)i\|\theta\|_{\infty}:=\max_{i}(\theta)_{i}. We now bound the error. By definition of the neighborhood Θn,2​δ/3​(θ0)\mathsf{\Theta}_{n,2\delta/3}(\theta_{0}) (20), we have

ϵtomo\displaystyle\epsilon_{\rm tomo} =𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐛[∥θ−θ0∥∞>n−1/2+δ/3]\displaystyle=\mathbf{Prob}\left[\|\theta-\theta_{0}\|_{\infty}>n^{-1/2+\delta/3}\right] (38)
≤𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐛[∥θ−θ^∥∞+∥θ^−θ0∥∞>n−1/2+δ/3]\displaystyle\leq\mathbf{Prob}\left[\|\theta-\hat{\theta}\|_{\infty}+\|\hat{\theta}-\theta_{0}\|_{\infty}>n^{-1/2+\delta/3}\right] (39)
≤𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐛[∥θ−θ^∥∞>n−1/2+δ/3(1−O(n−δ/3))].\displaystyle\leq\mathbf{Prob}\left[\|\theta-\hat{\theta}\|_{\infty}>n^{-1/2+\delta/3}(1-O(n^{-\delta/3}))\right]. (40)

The first inequality comes from triangle inequality and the second inequality is derived by noticing minθ≠θ′∈𝖫∥θ−θ′∥∞=(1/2)n−1/2\min_{\theta\not=\theta^{\prime}\in\mathsf{L}}\|\theta-\theta^{\prime}\|_{\infty}=(1/2)n^{-1/2}, which implies that ∥θ^−θ0∥∞≤(1/2)n−1/2\|\hat{\theta}-\theta_{0}\|_{\infty}\leq(1/2)n^{-1/2}. To further bound the error, we notice that the parameter space Θ\mathsf{\Theta} allows for the Euclidean expansion of trace distance, namely that there exists a constant CC such that ‖ρθ−ρθ′‖1=C​‖θ−θ′‖∞+O⁡(‖θ−θ′‖∞2)\|\rho_{\theta}-\rho_{\theta^{\prime}}\|_{1}=C\|\theta-\theta^{\prime}\|_{\infty}+O(\|\theta-\theta^{\prime}\|_{\infty}^{2}). And thus we have

ϵtomo\displaystyle\epsilon_{\rm tomo} ≤𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐛[12∥ρθ−ρθ^∥1>(C/4)n−1/2+δ/3].\displaystyle\leq\mathbf{Prob}\left[\frac{1}{2}\|\rho_{\theta}-\rho_{\hat{\theta}}\|_{1}>(C/4)n^{-1/2+\delta/3}\right]. (41)

Substituting ϵ\epsilon with (C/4)n−1/2+δ/3(C/4)n^{-1/2+\delta/3} and nn with n1−δ/2n^{1-\delta/2} in Eq. (27) we have

ϵtomo\displaystyle\epsilon_{\rm tomo} =n−Ω⁡(nδ/6).\displaystyle=n^{-\Omega(n^{\delta/6})}. (42)

Next we look at the error of amplification, which can be further split into two terms: the term of classical mode amplification and the term of quantum mode amplification. We first analyze the classical term, which comes from the rescaling of the Gaussian distribution. This operation shifts the center of the normal distribution from γn−1​δ​μ\sqrt{\gamma_{n}^{-1}}\delta\mu (the classical part of Gn/γn,θG_{n/\gamma_{n},\theta}) to δ​μ\delta\mu, which coincides with that of Gn,θG_{n,\theta}, while it also deforms the covariance matrix from Iμ0I_{\mu_{0}} to γn​Iμ0\gamma_{n}I_{\mu_{0}}. As a result, we consider the difference of the following distributions: Nδ​μ,Iμ0N_{\delta\mu,I_{\mu_{0}}} and Nδ​μ,γn​Iμ0N_{\delta\mu,\gamma_{n}I_{\mu_{0}}}. As they have the same center, we may translate them both to the origin. The error is:

ϵclassical=\displaystyle\epsilon_{\rm classical}= ∫ℝd||2πIμ0|−1/2e−12​𝐱T​Iμ0−1​𝐱−|2πγnIμ0|−1/2e−12​γn​𝐱T​Iμ0−1​𝐱|d𝐱\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left||2\pi I_{\mu_{0}}|^{-1/2}e^{-\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{x}^{T}I_{\mu_{0}}^{-1}\mathbf{x}}-|2\pi\gamma_{n}I_{\mu_{0}}|^{-1/2}e^{-\frac{1}{2\gamma_{n}}\mathbf{x}^{T}I_{\mu_{0}}^{-1}\mathbf{x}}\right|d\mathbf{x} (43)
≤\displaystyle\leq |2πIμ0|−1/2∫ℝd|e−12​𝐱T​Iμ0−1​𝐱−e−12​γn​𝐱T​Iμ0−1​𝐱|d𝐱+2πn−δ/2∫ℝde−12​γn​𝐱T​Iμ0−1​𝐱d𝐱\displaystyle|2\pi I_{\mu_{0}}|^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left|e^{-\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{x}^{T}I_{\mu_{0}}^{-1}\mathbf{x}}-e^{-\frac{1}{2\gamma_{n}}\mathbf{x}^{T}I_{\mu_{0}}^{-1}\mathbf{x}}\right|d\mathbf{x}+2\pi n^{-\delta/2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}e^{-\frac{1}{2\gamma_{n}}\mathbf{x}^{T}I_{\mu_{0}}^{-1}\mathbf{x}}d\mathbf{x} (44)
≤\displaystyle\leq O(n−δ/2)∫ℝd𝐱TIμ0−1𝐱e−12​𝐱T​Iμ0−1​𝐱d𝐱\displaystyle O(n^{-\delta/2})\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathbf{x}^{T}I_{\mu_{0}}^{-1}\mathbf{x}e^{-\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{x}^{T}I_{\mu_{0}}^{-1}\mathbf{x}}d\mathbf{x} (45)
=\displaystyle= O(n−δ/2)\displaystyle O(n^{-\delta/2}) (46)

Now we check the quantum term. On the quantum register, the amplifier acts independently on each mode as the displaced thermal state amplifier defined by Eq. (13). From a similar calculation as Eq. (15), we get that

ϵquantum≤12​∑j<k‖𝒜γn​(ραj,k,βj,k)−ραj,k,βj,k‖1,\displaystyle\epsilon_{\rm quantum}\leq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j<k}\left\|\mathcal{A}^{\gamma_{n}}\left(\rho_{\alpha_{j,k},\beta_{j,k}}\right)-\rho_{\alpha_{j,k},\beta_{j,k}}\right\|_{1}, (47)

where the error of each quantum amplifier is

12​‖𝒜γn​(ραj,k,βj,k)−ραj,k,βj,k‖1=\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathcal{A}^{\gamma_{n}}\left(\rho_{\alpha_{j,k},\beta_{j,k}}\right)-\rho_{\alpha_{j,k},\beta_{j,k}}\right\|_{1}= O(n−δ/2).\displaystyle O\left(n^{-\delta/2}\right). (48)

Therefore, we conclude that the amplification error scales at most as

ϵamp\displaystyle\epsilon_{\rm amp} ≤ϵclassical+ϵquantum=O(n−δ/2).\displaystyle\leq\epsilon_{\rm classical}+\epsilon_{\rm quantum}=O\left(n^{-\delta/2}\right). (49)

Let us now consider the term for the Gaussian state compression, which can be expressed as

ϵG≤\displaystyle\epsilon_{\rm G}\leq 12​‖𝒫c​(Nδ​μ,Iμ0)−Nδ​μ,Iμ0‖1+12​∑j<k‖𝒫nδ​(ραj,k,βj,k)−ραj,k,βj,k‖1\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathcal{P}_{\rm c}\left(N_{\delta\mu,I_{\mu_{0}}}\right)-N_{\delta\mu,I_{\mu_{0}}}\right\|_{1}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j<k}\left\|\mathcal{P}_{n^{\delta}}\left(\rho_{\alpha_{j,k},\beta_{j,k}}\right)-\rho_{\alpha_{j,k},\beta_{j,k}}\right\|_{1} (50)

For the classical part, noticing that ‖δ​μ‖∞≤nδ/3\|\delta\mu\|_{\infty}\leq n^{\delta/3}, we have

‖𝒫c​(Nδ​μ,Iμ0)−Nδ​μ,Iμ‖1\displaystyle\left\|\mathcal{P}_{\rm c}\left(N_{\delta\mu,I_{\mu_{0}}}\right)-N_{\delta\mu,I_{\mu}}\right\|_{1} ≤∑‖u‖∞>nδNδ​μ,Iμ0​(u)\displaystyle\leq\sum_{\|u\|_{\infty}>n^{\delta}}N_{\delta\mu,I_{\mu_{0}}}(u) (51)
≤∑‖u−δ​μ‖∞>nδ−nδ/3Nδ​μ,Iμ0​(u)\displaystyle\leq\sum_{\|u-\delta\mu\|_{\infty}>n^{\delta}-n^{\delta/3}}N_{\delta\mu,I_{\mu_{0}}}(u) (52)
=e−Ω⁡(n2​δ)\displaystyle=e^{-\Omega(n^{2\delta})} (53)

where Nδ​μ,Iμ0​(u)N_{\delta\mu,I_{\mu_{0}}}(u) denotes the probability distribution function. For each of the quantum modes, employing Lemma 2, with NN substituted by nδn^{\delta} and |αj,k|=O⁡(nδ/3)|\alpha_{j,k}|=O(n^{\delta/3}), we have

12​‖𝒫j,k​(ραj,k,βj,k)−ραj,k,βj,k‖1=βj,kΩ⁡(nδ/8)+e−Ω⁡(nδ/4).\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathcal{P}_{j,k}\left(\rho_{\alpha_{j,k},\beta_{j,k}}\right)-\rho_{\alpha_{j,k},\beta_{j,k}}\right\|_{1}=\beta_{j,k}^{\Omega(n^{\delta/8})}+e^{-\Omega(n^{\delta/4})}. (54)

Substituting Eqs. (53) and (54) into Eq. (50), we have

ϵG=maxj<k⁡[(μ0)k(μ0)j]Ω⁡(nδ/8)+e−Ω⁡(nδ/4).\displaystyle\epsilon_{\rm G}=\max_{j<k}\left[\frac{(\mu_{0})_{k}}{(\mu_{0})_{j}}\right]^{\Omega(n^{\delta/8})}+e^{-\Omega(n^{\delta/4})}. (55)

Finally, we note that the error of the Q-LAN approximation, corresponding to the errors generated by the transformations between the input state and its Gaussian state approximation, is given by Eqs. (24) and (25) as

ϵQ−LAN\displaystyle\epsilon_{\rm Q-LAN} =O⁡(n−κ⁡(δ)).\displaystyle=O\left(n^{-\kappa(\delta)}\right). (56)

Summarizing the above bounds (42), (49), (55), (56) on each of the error terms, we conclude that the protocol generates an error which scales at most

ϵ=O(n−κ⁡(δ))+O(n−δ/2)\displaystyle\epsilon=O\left(n^{-\kappa(\delta)}\right)+O\left(n^{-\delta/2}\right) (57)

IV-C Memory cost.

There are three sources of memory cost: a classical memory of [(fc+fq)/2]​log⁡n[(f_{c}+f_{q})/2]\log n bits for the tomography outcome, a classical memory of fc​δ​log⁡nf_{c}\delta\log n bits for the classical part of the Gaussian state and a quantum memory of fq​δ​log⁡nf_{q}\delta\log n qubits for the quantum part of the Gaussian state. It takes (1/2+δ)​log⁡n(1/2+\delta)\log n bits to encode a classical free parameter and (1/2)​log⁡n(1/2)\log n bits plus δ​log⁡n\delta\log n qubits to encode a quantum free parameter.

From the above discussion we can see that the ratio between the quantum memory cost and the classical memory cost is

Rq/c=δ​fq(1/2+δ)​fc+(1/2)​fq,\displaystyle R_{q/c}=\frac{\delta f_{q}}{(1/2+\delta)f_{c}+(1/2)f_{q}}, (58)

which can be made close to zero when δ\delta is set close to zero. This result shows that the quantum memory cost can be made arbitrarily small compared to the classical memory cost.

V Necessity of a quantum memory.

From the previous discussion, we know that the quantum memory cost can be made small compared to the classical memory cost. It then natural to ask whether the quantum memory is necessary at all or it is enough to perform full tomography on the input state and to use only a classical memory. Here we show that compression with a fully classical memory cannot be faithful, for both displaced thermal states and qudit states. A quick glance sees that, if the memory is fully classical, the concatenation of the encoder and the decoder would be a measure-and-prepare channel. The problem is then turned into the error benchmark problem, i.e. the problem of finding the minimal worst case error for measure-and-prepare transmissions of a family of states. The error benchmark ϵc\epsilon_{\rm c} for a family of states {ρx}x∈𝖷\{\rho_{x}\}_{x\in\mathsf{X}} is defined as

ϵc​({ρx}x∈𝖷):=inf𝒞(MP)sup𝐗∈𝖷12​‖𝒞(MP)​(ρx)−ρx‖1\displaystyle\epsilon_{\rm c}\left(\{\rho_{x}\}_{x\in\mathsf{X}}\right):=\inf_{\mathcal{C}^{(\rm MP)}}\sup_{\mathbf{X}\in\mathsf{X}}\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathcal{C}^{(\rm MP)}(\rho_{x})-\rho_{x}\right\|_{1} (59)

where the infimum is taken over all measure-and-prepare quantum channels 𝒞(MP)\mathcal{C}^{(\rm MP)}.

Let us start from the nn identically prepared displaced thermal state case. From existing results [24], we already know that the error benchmark for displaced thermal states is strictly positive

ϵc​({ρα,β}α∈ℂ)=(2−β)−iβ−1−βiβ+1>0\displaystyle\epsilon_{\rm c}\left(\{\rho_{\alpha,\beta}\}_{\alpha\in\mathbb{C}}\right)=(2-\beta)^{-i_{\beta}-1}-\beta^{i_{\beta}+1}>0 (60)

where iβi_{\beta} is the integer part of −log(2−β)/logβ(2−β)-\log(2-\beta)/\log\beta(2-\beta). The idea is to show that any compression protocol for displaced thermal states must at least have an error ϵc​({ρα,β}α∈ℂ)\epsilon_{\rm c}\left(\{\rho_{\alpha,\beta}\}_{\alpha\in\mathbb{C}}\right) in the asymptotic limit of large nn.

Consider any compression protocol (ℰn,𝒟n)\left(\mathcal{E}_{n},\mathcal{D}_{n}\right) for {ρα,β⊗n}(β,α)∈Θ\{\rho^{\otimes n}_{\alpha,\beta}\}_{(\beta,\alpha)\in\mathsf{\Theta}} using only classical memory. Note that we assume without loss of generality that the point (β,α=0)(\beta,\alpha=0) and its neighborhood are contained in the interior of Θ\mathsf{\Theta} for some β\beta, otherwise the same argument applies up to a displacement operation. We can then fix this β\beta, and construct a measure-and-prepare channel 𝒞n(MP)\mathcal{C}^{(\rm MP)}_{n} for the displaced thermal state family {ρα,β}α∈ℂ\{\rho_{\alpha,\beta}\}_{\alpha\in\mathbb{C}} with the following operational description:

  1. 1.

    For any input ρα,β\rho_{\alpha,\beta}, first use a beam splitter to split the state into ρ1−t2​α,β⊗ρt​α,β\rho_{\sqrt{1-t^{2}}\alpha,\beta}\otimes\rho_{t\alpha,\beta} for t=n−1/8t=n^{-1/8}.

  2. 2.

    Apply the heterodyne measurement to the second system whose state is ρt​α,β\rho_{t\alpha,\beta}, obtaining the estimate α^\hat{\alpha} of α\alpha with the probability distribution Q⁡(α^|α)=(1−β)​exp⁡[−(1−β)​t2​|α^−α|2]Q(\hat{\alpha}|\alpha)=(1-\beta)\exp[-(1-\beta)t^{2}|\hat{\alpha}-\alpha|^{2}].

  3. 3.

    Apply the displacement 𝒟−1−t2​α^\mathcal{D}_{-\sqrt{1-t^{2}}\hat{\alpha}} to the first system. The resultant state is ρ1−t2​(α−α^),β\rho_{\sqrt{1-t^{2}}(\alpha-\hat{\alpha}),\beta}.

  4. 4.

    Use beam splitters to transform the state into ρα′,β⊗n\rho_{\alpha^{\prime},\beta}^{\otimes n}, where α′=1−t2​(α−α^)/n\alpha^{\prime}=\sqrt{1-t^{2}}(\alpha-\hat{\alpha})/\sqrt{n}.

  5. 5.

    Apply 𝒟n∘ℰn\mathcal{D}_{n}\circ\mathcal{E}_{n}.

  6. 6.

    Use beam splitters to transform the state back into ρ1−t2​(α−α^),β\rho_{\sqrt{1-t^{2}}(\alpha-\hat{\alpha}),\beta} on the first mode.

    Apply the displacement 𝒟1−t2​α^\mathcal{D}_{\sqrt{1-t^{2}}\hat{\alpha}} to the first system. The resultant state is (approximately) ρ1−t2​α,β\rho_{\sqrt{1-t^{2}}\alpha,\beta}.

    Apply the amplifier 𝒜γt\mathcal{A}^{\gamma_{t}} (13) with γt=1/1−t2\gamma_{t}=1/\sqrt{1-t^{2}}.

The error of the above protocol can be bounded as

12​‖𝒞n(MP)​(ρα,β)−ρα,β‖1\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\|\mathcal{C}_{n}^{(\rm MP)}(\rho_{\alpha,\beta})-\rho_{\alpha,\beta}\|_{1} ≤∫1−t2​|α^−α|>n1/4Q⁡(dα^|α)+12​‖𝒜γt​(ρ1−t2​α,β)−ρα,β‖1\displaystyle\leq\int_{\sqrt{1-t^{2}}|\hat{\alpha}-\alpha|>n^{1/4}}Q(\mathop{\rm d}\nolimits\hat{\alpha}|\alpha)+\frac{1}{2}\|\mathcal{A}^{\gamma_{t}}(\rho_{\sqrt{1-t^{2}}\alpha,\beta})-\rho_{\alpha,\beta}\|_{1}
+12supα′:1−t2​|α^−α|≤n1/4∥𝒟n∘ℰn(ρα′,β⊗n)−ρα′,β⊗n∥1\displaystyle\qquad+\frac{1}{2}\sup_{\alpha^{\prime}:\sqrt{1-t^{2}}|\hat{\alpha}-\alpha|\leq n^{1/4}}\|\mathcal{D}_{n}\circ\mathcal{E}_{n}(\rho_{\alpha^{\prime},\beta}^{\otimes n})-\rho_{\alpha^{\prime},\beta}^{\otimes n}\|_{1}
≤e−Ω⁡(n1/4)+O(n−1/4)+12supα′:1−t2​|α^−α|≤n1/4∥𝒟n∘ℰn(ρα′,β⊗n)−ρα′,β⊗n∥1.\displaystyle\leq e^{-\Omega(n^{1/4})}+O(n^{-1/4})+\frac{1}{2}\sup_{\alpha^{\prime}:\sqrt{1-t^{2}}|\hat{\alpha}-\alpha|\leq n^{1/4}}\|\mathcal{D}_{n}\circ\mathcal{E}_{n}(\rho_{\alpha^{\prime},\beta}^{\otimes n})-\rho_{\alpha^{\prime},\beta}^{\otimes n}\|_{1}.

For large enough nn the set {(β,α′)|α′=1−t2(α−α^)/n,1−t2|α^−α|≤n1/4}={(β,α′)||α′|≤n−1/4}\{(\beta,\alpha^{\prime})~|~\alpha^{\prime}=\sqrt{1-t^{2}}(\alpha-\hat{\alpha})/\sqrt{n},\sqrt{1-t^{2}}|\hat{\alpha}-\alpha|\leq n^{1/4}\}=\{(\beta,\alpha^{\prime})~|~|\alpha^{\prime}|\leq n^{-1/4}\} is contained in Θ\mathsf{\Theta}, and thus we have

12​‖𝒞n(MP)​(ρα,β)−ρα,β‖1\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\|\mathcal{C}_{n}^{(\rm MP)}(\rho_{\alpha,\beta})-\rho_{\alpha,\beta}\|_{1} ≤e−Ω⁡(n1/4)+O(n−1/4)+12supα′∥𝒟n∘ℰn(ρα′,β⊗n)−ρα′,β⊗n∥1.\displaystyle\leq e^{-\Omega(n^{1/4})}+O(n^{-1/4})+\frac{1}{2}\sup_{\alpha^{\prime}}\|\mathcal{D}_{n}\circ\mathcal{E}_{n}(\rho_{\alpha^{\prime},\beta}^{\otimes n})-\rho_{\alpha^{\prime},\beta}^{\otimes n}\|_{1}.

≥(2−β)−iβ−1−βiβ+1>0.\displaystyle\geq(2-\beta)^{-i_{\beta}-1}-\beta^{i_{\beta}+1}>0.

This proves that (ℰn,𝒟n)(\mathcal{E}_{n},\mathcal{D}_{n}) is not faithful, and thus displaced thermal states cannot be compressed faithfully using only a classical memory.

The same idea can also be used for identically prepared qudit states thanks to Q-LAN. Namely that we can bound the performance of compression protocols for qudits limited to classical memories with the benchmark (60), using Q-LAN to interconvert between qudits and displaced thermal states.

Consider any compression protocol (ℰn,𝒟n)(\mathcal{E}_{n},\mathcal{D}_{n}) for the qudit family {ρθ⊗n}θ∈Θ\{\rho_{\theta}^{\otimes n}\}_{\theta\in\mathsf{\Theta}} (note that the parametrization is the same as in Eq. 2) using only a classical memory. We can lower bound its error by constructing a measure-and-prepare ℳn(MP)\mathcal{M}^{(\rm MP)}_{n} for the displaced thermal state family {ρα,β}α∈ℂ\{\rho_{\alpha,\beta}\}_{\alpha\in\mathbb{C}}, which uses (ℰn,𝒟n)(\mathcal{E}_{n},\mathcal{D}_{n}) as a subroutine. Choose θ0=(μ0,ξ0)\theta_{0}=(\mu_{0},\xi_{0}) such that its neighborhood is in Θ\mathsf{\Theta}, and then choose β=(μ0)k0/(μ0)j0\beta=(\mu_{0})_{k_{0}}/(\mu_{0})_{j_{0}} for some j0<k0j_{0}<k_{0}. ℳn(MP)\mathcal{M}^{(\rm MP)}_{n} consists in the following steps:

  1. 1.

    For any input ρα,β\rho_{\alpha,\beta}, first use a beam splitter to split the state into ρ1−t2​α,β⊗ρt​α,β\rho_{\sqrt{1-t^{2}}\alpha,\beta}\otimes\rho_{t\alpha,\beta} for t=n−1/11t=n^{-1/11}.

    Construct the following classical-quantum Gaussian state similar to Eq. (21) with δ​θ=0\delta\theta=0:

    G=N0,Iμ0​⨂j<kρj,kG=N_{0,I_{\mu_{0}}}\bigotimes_{j<k}\rho_{j,k}

    except that ρj0,k0\rho_{j_{0},k_{0}} is replaced by the resultant state in the previous step. ρj,k=ρ(μ0)k/(μ0)j(thm)\rho_{j,k}=\rho^{({\rm thm})}_{(\mu_{0})_{k}/(\mu_{0})_{j}} for (j,k)≠(j0,k0)(j,k)\neq(j_{0},k_{0}).

  5. 5.

    Apply the inverse Q-LAN transformation 𝒮θ0(n)\mathcal{S}^{(n)}_{\theta_{0}} as defined in Eq. (25).

    Apply the displacement 𝒟1−t2​α^\mathcal{D}_{\sqrt{1-t^{2}}\hat{\alpha}} to the system. The resultant state is (approximately) ρ1−t2​α,β\rho_{\sqrt{1-t^{2}}\alpha,\beta}.

    Apply the amplifier 𝒜tγ\mathcal{A}^{\gamma}_{t} (13) with γt=1/1−t2\gamma_{t}=1/\sqrt{1-t^{2}}.

Now we argue that the error of ℳn(MP)\mathcal{M}^{(\rm MP)}_{n} equals to the error of (𝒟n,ℰn)(\mathcal{D}_{n},\mathcal{E}_{n}), up to terms vanishing in the limit of large nn. We only need to justify that the error of Q-LAN transformations vanishes, since the error analysis for the other parts have already been done in the nn identically prepared displaced thermal state case.

Define the following neighborhood as in Eq. (20) with x=1/5x=1/5:

Θn,x(θ0)={θ=θ0+δθ/n,|∥δθ∥≤n110},\displaystyle\mathsf{\Theta}_{n,x}(\theta_{0})=\left\{\theta=\theta_{0}+\delta\theta/\sqrt{n},~|~\|\delta\theta\|\leq n^{\frac{1}{10}}\right\}\,, (61)

The probability that θ∉Θn,x​(θ0)\theta\notin\mathsf{\Theta}_{n,x}(\theta_{0}) is

𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐛[θ∉Θn,x(θ0)]≤\displaystyle\mathbf{Prob}\left[\theta\notin\mathsf{\Theta}_{n,x}(\theta_{0})\right]\leq 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐛[2(μ0)j−(μ0)k1−t2|α−α^|>n110]\displaystyle\mathbf{Prob}\left[2\sqrt{(\mu_{0})_{j}-(\mu_{0})_{k}}\sqrt{1-t^{2}}|\alpha-\hat{\alpha}|>n^{\frac{1}{10}}\right]
=\displaystyle= e−Ω⁡(n1/55).\displaystyle e^{-\Omega(n^{1/55})}.

using the tail of Gaussian distribution where the variance of (α^−α)(\hat{\alpha}-\alpha) is O⁡(n2/11)O(n^{2/11}). In the limit n→∞n\to\infty, using Eq. (60) we have

12​limn→∞supα′‖𝒟n∘ℰn​(ρα′,β⊗n)−ρα′,β⊗n‖1≥(2−β)−iβ−1−βiβ+1>0.\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\lim_{n\to\infty}\sup_{\alpha^{\prime}}\|\mathcal{D}_{n}\circ\mathcal{E}_{n}(\rho_{\alpha^{\prime},\beta}^{\otimes n})-\rho_{\alpha^{\prime},\beta}^{\otimes n}\|_{1}\geq(2-\beta)^{-i_{\beta}-1}-\beta^{i_{\beta}+1}>0.

This proves that displaced thermal states cannot be compressed faithfully using only a classical memory.

VI Optimality of the compression

The optimality proof of the compression protocol requires us to quantify the capacity of ensembles of ρθ⊗n\rho_{\theta}^{\otimes n}, i.e. to find an ensemble {pθ,ρθ⊗n}\{p_{\theta},\rho_{\theta}^{\otimes n}\} with large enough Holevo information [25] χ:=S⁡(∑θpθ​ρθ⊗n)−∑θpθ​S​(ρθ⊗n)\chi:=S(\sum_{\theta}p_{\theta}\rho_{\theta}^{\otimes n})-\sum_{\theta}p_{\theta}S(\rho_{\theta}^{\otimes n}) [S⁡(⋅)S(\cdot) denotes the von Neumann entropy]. Since any protocol requires a memory of size log⁡nenc≈log⁡χ\log n_{\rm enc}\approx\log\chi to encode the ensemble faithfully, we can get a good lower bound on nencn_{\rm enc}. We notice that the parameter space Θ\mathsf{\Theta} allows for the Euclidean expansion of trace distance, namely that there exists a constant CC such that ‖ρθ−ρθ′‖1=C​‖θ−θ′‖∞+O⁡(‖θ−θ′‖∞2)\|\rho_{\theta}-\rho_{\theta^{\prime}}\|_{1}=C\|\theta-\theta^{\prime}\|_{\infty}+O(\|\theta-\theta^{\prime}\|_{\infty}^{2}). Now we define a mesh 𝖬\mathsf{M} on the parameter space Θ\mathsf{\Theta}, on which points can be almost perfectly distinguished from each other:

𝖬={θ∈Θ||(θ−θ0)i|=zi⋅logn/n,zi∈ℕ∀i}\displaystyle\mathsf{M}=\left\{\theta\in\mathsf{\Theta}~|~|(\theta-\theta_{0})_{i}|=z_{i}\cdot\log n/\sqrt{n},z_{i}\in\mathbb{N}\ \forall\ i\right\} (62)

where θ0∈Θ\theta_{0}\in\mathsf{\Theta} is a fixed point. The mesh 𝖬\mathsf{M} is so defined that

ϵmin:=minθ≠θ′∈𝖬⁡12​‖ρθ−ρθ′‖1=C​log⁡n2​n+O⁡(log2⁡nn).\displaystyle\epsilon_{\min}:=\min_{\theta\not=\theta^{\prime}\in\mathsf{M}}\frac{1}{2}\|\rho_{\theta}-\rho_{\theta^{\prime}}\|_{1}=\frac{C\log n}{2\sqrt{n}}+O\left(\frac{\log^{2}n}{n}\right). (63)

On the other hand, the number of points contained in the mesh satisfies

|𝖬|≥TΘ​[nlog⁡n]fc+fq,\displaystyle|\mathsf{M}|\geq T_{\mathsf{\Theta}}\left[\frac{\sqrt{n}}{\log n}\right]^{f_{c}+f_{q}}, (64)

where TΘ>0T_{\mathsf{\Theta}}>0 is independent of nn. We consider an ensemble of states with parameters uniformly distributed in 𝖬\mathsf{M}, defined as

𝖢n={ρθ⊗n,∑θ0∈𝖬|𝖬|−1​δθ0,θ}.\displaystyle\mathsf{C}_{n}=\left\{\rho_{\theta}^{\otimes n},\sum_{\theta_{0}\in\mathsf{M}}|\mathsf{M}|^{-1}\delta_{\theta_{0},\theta}\right\}. (65)

We now show that the ensemble 𝖢n\mathsf{C}_{n} can be used to transmit log⁡|𝖬|\log|\mathsf{M}| bits of classical information almost perfectly. First of all, we notice that the states in 𝖢n\mathsf{C}_{n} are nearly perfectly distinguishable from each other. For qudit state subfamilies, define the following POVM elements distinguishing states as

M~θ\displaystyle\tilde{M}_{\theta} =∫12​‖σ−ρθ‖1≤ϵmin2dσ​Mσ\displaystyle=\int_{\frac{1}{2}\|\sigma-\rho_{\theta}\|_{1}\leq\frac{\epsilon_{\min}}{2}}\mathop{\rm d}\nolimits\sigma\,M_{\sigma} (66)

where MσM_{\sigma} is the qudit tomography POVM element defined in Eq. (9) of [23], which the property that

∫12​‖σ−ρ‖1≤ϵ/2dσ​Tr[Mσ​ρ⊗n]\displaystyle\int_{\frac{1}{2}\|\sigma-\rho\|_{1}\leq\epsilon/2}\mathop{\rm d}\nolimits\sigma\,\mathop{\rm Tr}\nolimits[M_{\sigma}\,\rho^{\otimes n}] ≥1−(n+1)3​d2​e−n​ϵ2.\displaystyle\geq 1-(n+1)^{3d^{2}}e^{-n\epsilon^{2}}. (67)

(For displaced thermal state families, a similar result holds for the heterodyne measurement of α\alpha and maximum likelihood estimation of β\beta [19].) The probability of error when this POVM is used to distinguish states in 𝖢n\mathsf{C}_{n} can be bounded as

Pe​(θ)\displaystyle P_{e}(\theta) =∫12​‖ρθ′−σ‖1>ϵmin2dσ​Tr[ρθ⊗n​Mσ]\displaystyle=\int_{\frac{1}{2}\|\rho_{\theta^{\prime}}-\sigma\|_{1}>\frac{\epsilon_{\min}}{2}}\mathop{\rm d}\nolimits\sigma\,\mathop{\rm Tr}\nolimits\left[\rho_{\theta}^{\otimes n}\,M_{\sigma}\right] (68)
≤(n+1)3​d2​e−C​log2​n4\displaystyle\leq(n+1)^{3d^{2}}e^{-\frac{C\log^{2}n}{4}} (69)
≤n−C​log⁡n8.\displaystyle\leq n^{-\frac{C\log n}{8}}. (70)

A communication protocol for conveying the message θ∈𝖬\theta\in\mathsf{M} is to transmit the quantum state ρm⊗n\rho_{m}^{\otimes n} and then to get the recovered message θ^\hat{\theta} using the POVM {M~θ}\{\tilde{M}_{\theta}\}. By Fano’s inequality [26], the Holevo information of the ensemble can be lower bounded as

χ⁡(𝖢n)\displaystyle\chi(\mathsf{C}_{n}) ≥I⁡(Θ:Θ^)\displaystyle\geq I(\Theta:\hat{\Theta}) (71)
≥(1−Pe)​log⁡|𝖬|−h⁡(Pe)\displaystyle\geq(1-P_{e})\log|\mathsf{M}|-h(P_{e}) (72)
=fc+fq2​log⁡n−(fc+fq)​log⁡log⁡n+o⁡(1).\displaystyle=\frac{f_{c}+f_{q}}{2}\log n-(f_{c}+f_{q})\log\log n+o(1). (73)

where S⁡(ρ)S(\rho) denotes the von Neumann entropy, h⁡(x)=−x​log⁡xh(x)=-x\log x (h⁡(0):=0h(0):=0), and

Pe=∫d⁡θ​Pe​(θ)∫d⁡θ≤n−C​log⁡n8\displaystyle P_{e}=\frac{\int\mathop{\rm d}\nolimits\theta\,P_{e}(\theta)}{\int\mathop{\rm d}\nolimits\theta}\leq n^{-\frac{C\log n}{8}} (74)

is the average error probability.

Finally, using the bound for quantum compression [27] we conclude that the number of qubits required is lower bounded as

nenc\displaystyle n_{\rm enc} ≥fc+fq2​log⁡n−(fc+fq)​log​log⁡n+h⁡(ϵ)+h⁡(1−ϵ)+O⁡(ϵ​log​n).\displaystyle\geq\frac{f_{c}+f_{q}}{2}\log n-(f_{c}+f_{q})\log\log n+h(\epsilon)+h(1-\epsilon)+O(\epsilon\log n). (75)

For ϵ\epsilon vanishing faster than the inverse of log⁡n\log n, the leading order of the compression cost is [(fc+fq)/2]​log⁡n[(f_{c}+f_{q})/2]\log n, which justifies the optimality of our protocol.

VII Conclusion

In this work we have solved the problem of compressing identically prepared states of finite-dimensional quantum systems and identically prepared displaced thermal states. We showed that the size of the required memory is proportional to the number of free parameters of the state. Especially, we note that finite-dimensional states can be stored in an almost-classical memory. Our compression protocol can be applied to study a quantum version of the problem of population coding, in the simple scenario where the population consists of identical and independently prepared quantum particles. However, in a real microscopic system, particles typically have correlation. An interesting and challenging problem, left to future research, is the extension of our results to the study of correlated quantum manybody systems.

-A Proof of Lemma 1.

For any x>0x>0, we define a series of t+1=⌊n1/2+x⌋t+1=\lfloor n^{1/2+x}\rfloor intervals 𝖫0,…​𝖫t\mathsf{L}_{0},\dots\mathsf{L}_{t} as

𝖫0\displaystyle\mathsf{L}_{0} ={0}\displaystyle=\{0\}
𝖫i\displaystyle\mathsf{L}_{i} ={(i−1)​⌊n(1−x)/2⌋+1,…,i⁡⌊n(1−x)/2⌋}0<i<t\displaystyle=\{(i-1)\,\lfloor n^{(1-x)/2}\rfloor+1,\dots,i\,\lfloor n^{(1-x)/2}\rfloor\}\quad 0<i<t
𝖫t\displaystyle\mathsf{L}_{t} ={(t−1)​⌊n(1−x)/2⌋+1,…}.\displaystyle=\{(t-1)\,\lfloor n^{(1-x)/2}\rfloor+1,\dots\}.

For any non-negative integer mm, we denote by i⁡(m)i(m) the index of the interval containing mm, i.e. m∈𝖫i⁡(m)m\in\mathsf{L}_{i(m)}.

To design the compression protocol, we first notice that the nn-fold thermal state can be written in the form

(ρβ(thm))⊗n=(1−β)n​∑m→β|m→|​|m→⟩​⟨m→|,\displaystyle\left(\rho^{({\rm thm})}_{\beta}\right)^{\otimes n}=(1-\beta)^{n}\sum_{\vec{m}}\beta^{|\vec{m}|}|\vec{m}\rangle\langle\vec{m}|, (76)

where |m→⟩=|m1⟩⊗⋯⊗|mn⟩|\vec{m}\rangle=|m_{1}\rangle\otimes\cdots\otimes|m_{n}\rangle is the photon number basis of nn modes and |m→|:=m1+⋯+mn|\vec{m}|:=m_{1}+\cdots+m_{n}. The compression protocol runs as follows:

  • •

    Encoder. First perform projective measurement in the photon number basis of nn modes, which yields an nn-dimensional vector m→\vec{m}. Then compute i⁡(|m→|)i(|\vec{m}|) and encode it into a classical memory. The encoding channel can be represented as

    Decoder. Read an integer ii from the memory. If i≥ti\geq t prepare a fixed state |t→⟩​⟨t→||\vec{t}\rangle\langle\vec{t}| (defined below); if i<ti<t perform random sampling in the interval 𝖫i\mathsf{L}_{i}. For each outcome m^\hat{m} of the sampling, prepare the nn-mode state

    (n+m^−1m^)−1∑m→:|m→|=m^|m→⟩⟨m→|.{n+\hat{m}-1\choose\hat{m}}^{-1}\sum_{\vec{m}:|\vec{m}|=\hat{m}}|\vec{m}\rangle\langle\vec{m}|.

    Then the decoding channel can be represented as

    𝒟n,x(thm)​(|i⟩​⟨i|)\displaystyle\mathcal{D}^{({\rm thm})}_{n,x}\left(|i\rangle\langle i|\right) :={∑m→:|m→|∈𝖫i|m→⟩​⟨m→||𝖫i|​(n+|m→|−1|m→|)i<t|t→⟩​⟨t→|i=t\displaystyle:=\left\{\begin{matrix}\sum_{\vec{m}:|\vec{m}|\in\mathsf{L}_{i}}\frac{|\vec{m}\rangle\langle\vec{m}|}{|\mathsf{L}_{i}|{n+|\vec{m}|-1\choose|\vec{m}|}}&\quad i<t\\ |\vec{t}\rangle\langle\vec{t}|&\quad i=t\end{matrix}\right.
    t→\displaystyle\vec{t} =((t−1)​⌊n(1−x)/2⌋+1,…,(t−1)​⌊n(1−x)/2⌋+1).\displaystyle=((t-1)\,\lfloor n^{(1-x)/2}\rfloor+1,\dots,(t-1)\,\lfloor n^{(1-x)/2}\rfloor+1).

It is straightforward from definition that the protocol uses log⁡(t+1)=(1/2+x)​log⁡n+o⁡(1)\log(t+1)=(1/2+x)\log n+o(1) classical bits. What remains is to bound the error of the protocol. First, we notice that the recovered state is

(ρβ,n)m→\displaystyle\left(\rho_{\beta,n}\right)_{\vec{m}} ={(1−β)n​β|m→|​∑m∈𝖫i⁡(|m→|)βm−|m→|​(n+m−1m)|𝖫i⁡(|m→|)|​(n+|m→|−1|m→|)i⁡(|m→|)<t∑m→′:i⁡(|m→′|)=t(1−β)nβ|m→′|m→=t→0else.\displaystyle=\left\{\begin{matrix}(1-\beta)^{n}\beta^{|\vec{m}|}\sum_{m\in\mathsf{L}_{i(|\vec{m}|)}}\frac{\beta^{m-|\vec{m}|}{n+m-1\choose m}}{|\mathsf{L}_{i(|\vec{m}|)}|{n+|\vec{m}|-1\choose|\vec{m}|}}&\quad i(|\vec{m}|)<t\\ \\ \sum_{\vec{m}^{\prime}:i(|\vec{m}^{\prime}|)=t}(1-\beta)^{n}\beta^{|\vec{m}^{\prime}|}&\quad\vec{m}=\vec{t}\\ \\ 0&\quad\text{else}.\end{matrix}\right. (78)

We choose 𝖲\mathsf{S} as the minimal set satisfying OPENi)i) 𝖲\mathsf{S} is a union of several intervals chosen from the set {𝖫i}\{\mathsf{L}_{i}\} and ii)

𝖲⊃[β​n1−β−n(1−x)/2,β​n1−β+n(1−x)/2].\displaystyle\mathsf{S}\supset\left[\frac{\beta n}{1-\beta}-n^{(1-x)/2},\frac{\beta n}{1-\beta}+n^{(1-x)/2}\right]. (79)

≤∑m→:|m→|∉𝖲(1−β)nβ|m→|+12[∑m→:|m→|∈𝖲(1−β)nβ|m→|]maxm′∈𝖫i𝖫i∩𝖲≠∅|∑m∈𝖫iβm​(n+m−1m)|𝖫i|​βm′​(n+m′−1m′)−1|+∑m→′:i⁡(|m→′|)=t(1−β)nβ|m→′|\displaystyle\leq\sum_{\vec{m}:|\vec{m}|\not\in\mathsf{S}}(1-\beta)^{n}\beta^{|\vec{m}|}+\frac{1}{2}\left[\sum_{\vec{m}:|\vec{m}|\in\mathsf{S}}(1-\beta)^{n}\beta^{|\vec{m}|}\right]\max_{\tiny\begin{matrix}m^{\prime}\in\mathsf{L}_{i}\\ \mathsf{L}_{i}\cap\mathsf{S}\not=\emptyset\end{matrix}}\left|\sum_{m\in\mathsf{L}_{i}}\frac{\beta^{m}{n+m-1\choose m}}{|\mathsf{L}_{i}|\beta^{m^{\prime}}{n+m^{\prime}-1\choose m^{\prime}}}-1\right|+\sum_{\vec{m}^{\prime}:i(|\vec{m}^{\prime}|)=t}(1-\beta)^{n}\beta^{|\vec{m}^{\prime}|}
